items.title: Chang'e-6 Samples Reveal the Violent Chain Reaction That Built the Moon’s Largest Crater
items.blurb: One of the most prominent features on the Moon is one we can’t regularly see, at least not completely. The South Pole-Aitken (SPA) basin is one of the largest, oldest, and deepest impact craters on the Moon, and until recently we’ve only been able to observe it from afar - and even then only when we sent orbiters around to the far side, which is never in direct line of sight with the Earth. Recently China has been busily sending landers and rovers to the site, and a new paper, published in Science Advances, details the actual samples returned to Earth by the Chang’e-6 mission and combines them with the in-situ data from the Chang’e-4 mission and rover. Those details combine to form a complete geological history of the major impacts that formed the basin, and some insight into the age of other impact craters scattered throughout the solar system.

However, the extent to which these models can predict functional transporter inhibition remains unclear. Here, we systematically evaluated the predictive utility of structural metrics generated by AlphaFold3, Boltz-2, Chai-1, and Protenix using experimental inhibition measurements for 224 compounds across OATP1B1, OATP1B3, and OATP2B1. Individual structural metrics provided substantial inhibitor discrimination ability, reaching an ROC-AUC of 0.888 for Chai-1 structures of OATP1B3. We then investigated whether integrating multiple structural descriptors improves inhibitor classification relative to optimized individual metrics, which improved performances in many model-OATP combinations. Following combined-metric analysis, Protenix exhibited both the highest absolute average precision (AP) and the largest improvement in AP overall for OATP1B1 (0.560 to 0.763). Mean improvements persisted across five independently generated cross validation partitions. Performance and the benefits of metric integration differed across transporters and modeling pipelines, while increasing structural ensemble size for each drug from 1 to 100 provided varied improvements. Together, these findings establish the utility of co-folding structural metrics as functional classification features, and this work establishes a framework for evaluating and integrating structure-prediction outputs in broader functional studies of membrane transporters.

items.title: Cyst-like intraluminal hyaluronic acid accumulation inhibits breast epithelial cell invasion via pressure-driven ECM compaction
items.blurb: While elevated hyaluronic acid (HA) biosynthesis by breast epithelial cells is implicated in tumorigenesis, HA can also contribute to benign tissue remodeling, including mammary morphogenesis and lumen formation in embryogenesis. What determines whether HA drives malignant invasion or benign remodeling remains unclear. To investigate, we embedded spheroids of HA synthase (HAS)-overexpressing breast epithelial cells in collagen hydrogels modeling dense breast stroma. Confocal and optical coherence microscopy showed that HAS overexpression produced different outcomes in single cells and spheroids: individual cells invaded into the collagen, whereas spheroids accumulated HA internally, causing osmotic swelling and hydrostatic pressure-driven lumen formation. An in silico cell-vertex model identified paracellular fluid flow as a mechanism of lumen formation, coinciding with confinement-induced reorganization of cell-cell adhesion strengths. In situ pressure sensors, confocal reflectance imaging, and finite element analysis showed that spheroid expansion compressed the surrounding collagen, inducing densification and a material phase transition that inhibited invasion. Co-culture and direct contact with matrix-remodeling stromal cells attenuated this effect and restored invasive potential. Although HA overproduction in single cells has been linked to malignancy, our findings identify a biophysical mechanism by which multicellular HA accumulation suppresses tumor invasion and show how stromal remodeling can override this protection. These results offer a potential explanation for the context-dependent relationship between fibrocystic breast changes and breast cancer risk.

items.title: Identification of Functional NOD2-Specific Aptamers Using APT-SNAP Microarrays to Screen Zebrafish Nod-like Receptors
items.blurb: NOD-like receptors (NLRs) are intracellular immune sensors that monitor for pathogen- and damage-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs, DAMPs) and initiate innate immune signaling pathways upon detection. Dysregulation of NLR signaling contributes to numerous inflammatory diseases and cancers, yet mechanistic studies of NLR proteins are limited by the availability of reliable detection reagents, particularly in emerging model organisms such as zebrafish (Danio rerio). Although zebrafish provide a powerful system for studying innate immunity, few validated antibodies exist for zebrafish NLR proteins. Here, we describe the development of aptamer-based detection reagents targeting zebrafish NLRs using the APT-SNAP platform, a high-density aptamer microarray technology that enables rapid identification of protein-binding nucleic acid ligands. Using this approach, we identified multiple DNA aptamers that bind zebrafish NLR proteins and selected candidates targeting NOD2 for further characterization. Orthogonal validation assays, which include enzyme-linked apta-sorbent assays (ELASAs), pull-downs, biolayer interferometry (BLI), and fluorescence microscopy, confirmed that the lead aptamers bind zebrafish NOD2 with high affinity and specificity, and function effectively in biochemical and cellular assays. These results demonstrate that APT-SNAP generated validated, native-state affinity reagents for a zebrafish immune protein where commercial antibodies failed, providing new molecular tools for investigating NLR biology in zebrafish. More broadly, this strategy establishes a generalizable approach for generating affinity reagents against challenging protein targets that lack reliable antibodies.

items.title: Pseudo-helicase motifs of SecA involved in ATP-driven dynamic coupling for protein translocation
items.blurb: The ubiquitous Sec translocon is a highly conserved machine specialised for polypeptide translocation through lipid bilayers. In the bacterial system, the cytoplasmic motor ATPase SecA associates with the core channel complex SecYEG, through which unfolded polypeptides are driven across the membrane by a Brownian ratchet mechanism. How the energy released during the ATP-hydrolytic cycle is transduced to the conformational changes required for preprotein secretion is not well understood. Here, we re-explore the known homology between SecA and the nucleic acid helicases to better understand the fundamentals of dynamic energy coupling during biopolymer transport: how ATP-turnover is regulated by the engaged polypeptide, and how the ensuing conformational changes bring about transport. Using bioinformatics and comparative structural analysis we identify several motifs within SecA equivalent to those required for helicase activity. We then probe their involvement in protein translocation experimentally by site specific amino acid substitution and the analysis of reconstituted variant activity. The results show that the pseudo-helicase translocation motifs are important for regulating ATP-coupled protein transport, enabling the motor to sense and respond to the translocating polypeptide.

items.title: Sugar Matters: How Protein Glycosylation Shapes Ligand Binding
items.blurb: Altered protein glycosylation accompanies many diseases and can influence drug binding, yet the contributions of specific glycan features remain difficult to resolve within heterogeneous glycoprotein populations. Here, we combined sequential enzymatic glycan remodeling, composition-resolved variable-temperature native mass spectrometry (vT-nMS), complementary glycosylation analyses, and molecular modelling to investigate warfarin binding to the F1 and S variants of human 1-acid glycoprotein (AGP). Measured affinities spanned more than an order of magnitude across the glycan compositions and remodeled samples examined. Core 1-6 fucosylation favored binding by both variants and shifted the thermodynamics toward less favorable enthalpy and more favorable entropy. Antennary fucosylation generally weakened binding in F1 and had more variable effects in S. Weaker binding was associated with a less favorable entropic contribution despite more favorable enthalpy. Outer-arm trimming produced variant-dependent effects, including changes in enthalpic and entropic contributions that were partly obscured by comparatively small changes in affinity. Endo F3-mediated truncation also produced distinct responses in the two variants. Within the F1 truncation series, the three-core population exhibited the strongest binding and greatest enthalpic stabilization, whereas the corresponding S population exhibited a more favorable entropic contribution than F1 without a comparable affinity enhancement. No warfarin complexes were detected for compositions assigned as containing bisecting GlcNAc. Molecular simulations and reconstructed glycan ensembles suggested that changes in glycan orientation and glycan-protein interactions near the binding-funnel entrance may contribute to the observed binding effects. Together, these findings reveal how glycan structure and protein sequence jointly determine the affinity and thermodynamic balance of ligand recognition and demonstrate the value of composition-resolved vT-nMS for dissecting functional heterogeneity in glycoprotein populations.

items.title: Not all DNase 1 are created equal
items.blurb: DNase I is a ubiquitous reagent, used to remove contaminating DNA from RNA preparations and other samples, and preparations from different suppliers are widely treated as interchangeable. Suppliers describe their products as improved --- faster, more complete, more stable --- but what better means is rarely defined in terms a user can reproduce: activity units are tied to each supplier's own assay, recommended protocols specify a single amount and a single time, and stability in storage, through freeze--thaw cycles and at working temperature, is seldom quantified. Here we adapt a low-cost fluorophore--quencher reporter of the kind used for Cas12 trans-cleavage diagnostics as a kinetic assay for DNase I, and compare preparations from three suppliers, each used at 1 U/ L, on plates that carry blanks, replicates and a standard of fully digested reporter. At large amounts (16--32 U) ThermoFisher and Zymo preparations were indistinguishable early in the reaction. At sub-saturating amounts ([≤]4 U) the product formed per labelled unit differed up to {approx}3.6-fold at 1 U (Zymo over ThermoFisher) and by considerably more at 0.25--0.5 U, where ThermoFisher signal was close to background. The ranking depended on dose, on time, and on whether rate or yield was the metric: from about 3 h onward ThermoFisher formed the least product at 1--4 U yet had the shortest fitted time constants, Synthego and Zymo were similar at [≤]1 U, and Synthego, slower to start, yielded more than Zymo after about 2--3 h at 4 U. On a single plate, two Zymo DNase I aliquots from different laboratories differed up to 19-fold at equal nominal volume. We argue that DNase I performance should be reported as calibrated dose--response and time-course data under stated conditions, with storage stability quantified, and that laboratories should verify the enzyme they actually hold. The reporter costs about $0.10 per reaction, is in principle readable on a simple LED fluorometer, and can be modified to probe dsDNA, RNA and nucleic-acid--binding proteins.

items.title: Antifungal and Antibiofilm Activity of a Thermostable Lipid Transfer Protein-Enriched Fraction from Capsicum annuum L. Seeds against Candidozyma auris
items.blurb: The emergence of multidrug-resistant Candidozyma auris (C. auris) has intensified the search for antifungal molecules with alternative structures and mechanisms of action. Here, we investigated Capsicum annuum L. seeds as a source of thermostable antifungal peptides. Thermal fractionation of a crude aqueous seed extract (RBPCE) yielded a heat-treated fraction (RBPHT) enriched in low-molecular-weight proteins. LC-MS/MS identified the type I and type II non-specific lipid-transfer proteins Ca-nsLTP1 and Ca-nsLTP2 as its predominant constituents. Compared with RBPCE, RBPHT displayed increased trypsin-inhibitory potency. RBPHT inhibited C. albicans, C. krusei, and C. auris isolates from clades I, III, and IV, including isolates showing no detectable response to fluconazole under the conditions tested. Against a representative South American clade IV isolate, the nsLTP-enriched fraction exhibited minimum inhibitory and fungicidal concentrations of 180 and 360 g/mL, respectively. RBPHT also suppressed early biofilm establishment by C. albicans and C. auris and markedly reduced viable biofilm-associated populations when applied after initial cell adhesion. These findings provide the first evidence of antifungal and antibiofilm activity by a Capsicum seed-derived nsLTP-enriched fraction against C. auris and position Ca-nsLTP1 and Ca-nsLTP2 as promising plant-derived candidates for further antifungal development.

items.title: Replication Protein A recognizes DNA junctions to spatially organize genome maintenance
items.blurb: Single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) intermediates arise during many DNA metabolic processes and are rapidly coated by the conserved ssDNA-binding protein Replication Protein A (RPA), which protects ssDNA and coordinates the recruitment of downstream DNA metabolic factors. However, how RPA directs the precise spatial recruitment of DNA metabolic proteins to RPA-coated DNA remains unclear. Here we show that RPA possesses an intrinsic preference for single-stranded/double-stranded DNA (ss/dsDNA) junctions, creating localized binding states that promote the junction-specific recruitment of incoming proteins. Junction-proximal RPA exhibits enhanced resistance to disassembly through conserved structural elements within its DNA-binding domains. RPA phosphorylation diminishes this junction preference, providing a mechanism for remodeling junction-associated complexes. We further demonstrate that RPA directly regulates the junction-specific loading and engagement of the nucleotide excision repair factor XPA. Together, these findings establish a mechanistic basis for RPA recognition of ss/dsDNA junctions and support a general framework in which RPA spatially organizes DNA metabolic factors at sites of ssDNA formation. More broadly, these findings resolve how proteins gain selective access to DNA embedded within RPA-coated intermediates and identify junction recognition as a previously unrecognized regulatory feature of RPA function.

items.title: Characterizing Material Mechanics and Modeling Variability in Organic Hydrogels: A Framework for Soft and Biodegradable Robotics
items.blurb: Organic hydrogels are increasingly used in biofabrication, soft robotics, and biomedical devices due to their tunable mechanical properties, biocompatibility, biodegradability, and flexible fabrication modalities, including embedded 3D printing. However, both polymer chemistry and fabrication conditions can introduce substantial variability in material behavior, particularly for biologically-derived polymers whose inconsistent molecular composition and cross-linking response affect viscoelastic performance. This variability complicates design, reduces reproducibility, and obscures the steady-state mechanical properties required for functional deployment. In this work, we present an experimental-computational framework for characterizing and predicting the mechanical behavior of 3D-printed hydrogels. The workflow characterizes material behavior across molecular, bulk, and population scales. First, we quantify intrinsic polymer variability via $^1$H-NMR spectroscopy to assess monomer distributions governing ionic cross-linking, establishing a molecular-level explanation for observed material variability. Next, we systematically measure how cross-linking time and temperature influence dynamic swelling and stiffness, highlighting representative conditions under which the material approaches steady-state mechanics while maintaining geometric fidelity. Finally, we develop a generative population model to describe geometry and stiffness evolution during cross-linking and calibrate its parameters using Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) methods, enabling prediction of population-level distributions and variability from limited experimental data. We demonstrate this framework using FRESH-printed sodium alginate constructs as a case study; alginate hydrogels approach steady-state swelling and stiffness after extended cross-linking (>8 hr), and elevated temperatures increase contraction without improving modulus, indicating that low-temperature, long-duration cross-linking enhances geometric and mechanical stability. By integrating molecular composition, fabrication-dependent variability, and dynamic cross-linking behavior into a probabilistic model, this framework provides a structured approach for researchers to quantify uncertainty and design around variability in organic hydrogels, supporting more predictable deployment of soft robotic actuators, tissue-mimetic constructs, and biodegradable devices.

items.title: Zeno Trap-enabled Quadrupole-Scanning Data-Independent Acquisition in nanoflow Quantitative Proteomics and Immunopeptidomics
items.blurb: We have investigated the quantitative and qualitative attributes of a scanning quadrupole data-independent acquisition (ZT Scan DIA) mode enabled on a SCIEX ZenoTOF 7600+ system using nanoflow chromatographic separations and targeted towards immunopeptidomic analysis. ZT Scan DIA incorporates increased ion utilization and MS/MS sensitivity introduced through the Zeno trapping modality, with quadrupole-resolved isolation windows in the data-independent acquisition mode. We demonstrate superior quantitative performance of ZT Scan DIA in sensitive nanoflow separations of tryptic peptides. Additionally, in LFQBench experiments, we demonstrate a remarkable quantitative accuracy and precision with experimentally measured precursor false-discovery rates below 1% using complex mixtures of yeast, human, and E. coli-derived tryptic digests when compared to conventional DIA experiments on the same platform. Having established its effectiveness in nanoflow proteomics analyses, we further investigated ZT Scan DIA for HLA-peptide characterization. These analyses highlighted the ability of the scanning quadrupole dimension to enrich the information needed for improved fragment-to-precursor assignment and quantitation of near-isobaric immunopeptides, should the search algorithms exploit it.

items.title: Dog Meets Man: Alloparenting and Affective Care within Co-Constructed Street Dog-Human Lifeworlds in Delhi, India
items.blurb: Rapid urbanisation and largely unplanned development in Indian cities have been drawing increasing ethnographic attention in recent years. Even though other-than-human beings are an integral part of these spaces, the city is still most often understood from a human perspective. Simultaneously, nonhumans actively shape and reshape their environments through everyday behavioural choices - choices that are not only ecological, but also socioeconomic, and often influenced by their interactions and relationships with human beings. In this paper, we adopt a mixed-methods, etho-ethnographic approach to explore a curious case of other-than-human alloparenting within largely affective dog - lifeworlds in the Indian megapolis of Delhi. We focus on a triadic relationship between two co-territorial female street dogs -- Bhuri and Kali -- and a particular human caregiver -- Kishan -- that reveal how these two dogs, sharing the same territory within Gur Mandi, an informal settlement in north Delhi, adjust their allo/parenting behaviour in response to their independent social interactions with the human residents of the area. This more-than-human narrative suggests that street dogs are not merely passive inhabitants of the city, but sentient, affective participants, who shape urban life through their everyday interactions. Moreover, the counter-intuitive shifts that we observed in multibeing parenting behaviour reflect how human presence could configure short-term social interactions and the long-term relationships between nonhuman beings in their shared spaces.

items.title: Chromosome-scale genome assembly of multinucleate heterokaryotic Rhizoctonia solani AG1-IB
items.blurb: Rhizoctonia solani AG1-IB is an economically important fungal pathogen of turfgrass and agricultural crops, yet available genome assemblies remain fragmented or represent collapsed or consensus sequences that obscure haplotype-specific variation, limiting investigations of genome evolution and heterokaryosis. Here, we present a chromosome-scale, haplotype-aware genome assembly of AG1-IB isolate S1W6 generated using Oxford Nanopore sequencing, Hi-C scaffolding, and short-read polishing. De novo assembly with PECAT produced two haplotype-aware nuclear genome assemblies, with BUSCO completeness greater than 96% and nuclear genome N50 values exceeding 2 Mb. Comparative analyses revealed substantial haplotype divergence, with over 600,000 SNPs and 80,000 indels between haplotypes with 97.75% average nucleotide identity separating assemblies. FastANI analyses showed comparable genetic divergence between Hap1 and Hap2 assemblies of S1W6 to that observed among independently collected AG1-IB isolates from different plant hosts and geographic regions. Despite extensive nucleotide variation, Gene Ontology profiles, predicted effector repertoires, carbohydrate-active enzymes, and biosynthetic gene cluster composition were conserved between assemblies. In contrast, homeodomain (HD) mating-type loci were variable. Hap2 contained four HD genes (W-HD1, W-HD2, E-HD1, and E-HD2), whereas Hap1 lacked E-HD1, and shared divergent HD amino acid sequences. A STE3 pheromone receptor gene on chromosome 15 was highly conserved in both haplotypes. This study provides the first chromosome-scale, haplotype-resolved genome resource for R. solani AG1-IB and demonstrates that heterokaryotic individuals can harbor genomic variation approaching the levels observed among genetically diverse isolates of AG1-IB. These findings highlight the importance of haplotype-aware assemblies for understanding genome evolution and mating-type diversity in heterokaryotic fungal plant pathogens.

items.title: Reproductive fitness does not predict plastic changes in recombination due to diet in Drosophila melanogaster
items.blurb: Meiotic recombination is a fundamental biological process that ensures proper chromosome segregation and generates novel genetic variation. Recombination rate exhibits plasticity in response to environmental conditions, yet how genetic background interacts with nutrition to influence this plasticity remains poorly understood. Using Drosophila melanogaster lines from the Drosophila Genetic Reference Panel (DGRP), we evaluated how varying caloric density affects X-chromosome recombination, body mass, fecundity, and survival across genotypes and over time. Caloric restriction significantly reduced female body mass in both genotypes, indicating a shared physiological response to dietary manipulation. Dietary treatment did not significantly affect egg-to-adult survival in marker-free crosses, whereas the high-calorie diet significantly reduced survival in marker-present crosses. After accounting for differential viability, we detected a significant genotype-by-environment (GE) interaction in X-chromosome recombination rates. Furthermore, shifts in recombination rate were not associated with reduced survival or fecundity, failing to support adaptive hypotheses as explanations for recombination plasticity. To assess overall ovarian gene expression during these dietary perturbations, we conducted ovarian transcriptomic profiling (RNA-seq) . Ovarian gene expression analysis revealed distinct, genotype-specific transcriptional responses to caloric restriction and excess calories, including significant changes in metabolic, stress-response, and cellular maintenance pathways across early and late time points. Overall, these findings demonstrate genotype-dependent recombination plasticity in response to dietary variation, without a consistent relationship between recombination rate and measured components of reproductive fitness, providing no support for the prediction of fitness-associated recombination under the dietary conditions examined. This work highlights the complex relationship of recombination rate plasticity among genotype, environment, and reproductive traits.

items.title: Genetic Diversity and Geographic Structure of Nordic Rye Landraces and Historic Varieties: Expected Patterns and New Insights
items.blurb: Rye has been an important food crop and source of nutrition in Finland for centuries and remains so today. Rye landraces and old varieties are still grown on farmers' fields. Interest in local landraces and conservation varieties has grown during the last decade due to climate change and its negative effects on biodiversity and resilience. We explored genetic diversity and population structure in Nordic rye landraces, historic population varieties and reference materials using complementary SSR and SNP datasets. For comparative analysis of genetic diversity, the Finnish varieties 'Riihi' and 'Reetta', the German inbred line Lo7, a German hybrid variety, the Estonian variety 'Elvi', and the landrace 'Sangaste' were included as reference materials. Both SSR and SNP analyses revealed geographically associated genetic differentiation within an otherwise largely shared Nordic rye gene pool. Notably, the independently sampled Mustialan and NordGen accessions of the Norwegian 'Tvengsberg' landrace were each clearly differentiated from the remaining rye material in the SSR and SNP datasets, respectively. Finnish landraces ('Aunus', 'Hermanni', 'Iivo', 'Joppe', 'Paakkola', and 'Taavetti') showed broadly similar genetic profiles, although substantial admixture was evident. In the SSR analysis, the Estonian accessions 'Sangaste' and 'Elvi' clustered together with 'Reetta', 'Riihi', and the Finnish landrace 'Polvijarvi', suggesting a closer genetic relationship among these accessions, although 'Polvijarvi' has previously been considered a distinct Finnish landrace. The Finnish variety 'Hankkijan Jussi' formed a separate cluster; this variety originates from a selection derived from the 60Co-irradiated Russian variety 'Vjatka'. The modern inbred line Lo7 and an unnamed hybrid variety were included as outgroup controls and showed clear genetic divergence from the Fennoscandian landrace material. Although Nordic rye landraces are often assumed to share a common ancestry and may have been influenced by historical seed exchange among farming communities, both SSR and SNP analyses revealed geographically associated genetic differentiation. These results indicate that regional genetic differentiation has been maintained despite the outcrossing nature of rye and the potential for historical gene flow.

items.title: Contrasting microhaplotype diversity responses of saproxylic beetles to forest management
items.blurb: Genetic responses to forest management may vary substantially among saproxylic beetles because species differ in habitat requirements, dispersal and ecological specialization. Here, we evaluated whether microhaplotypes reconstructed from Double Digest Restriction-site Associated DNA sequencing (ddRADseq) loci provide additional locus-level genetic information and reveal species-specific associations with forest protection, management and habitat characteristics across 12 saproxylic beetle species sampled in eight forest complexes in Poland. Phased combinations of linked Single Nucleotide Polymorphism (SNPs) within RAD loci were analysed as multi-allelic microhaplotypes. Observed microhaplotype diversity was compared with analytical expectations under linkage equilibrium to assess how diversity differed from that expected if constituent SNP positions were independent. Observed microhaplotype diversity was consistently lower than expected under linkage equilibrium across all 12 species, with the magnitude of the difference varying among species. Patterns of population differentiation inferred from SNP-based FST and microhaplotype-based {Phi}ST were significantly concordant in all species, although the strength of correspondence varied considerably among taxa. Individual microhaplotype homozygosity (FHAP) showed heterogeneous associations with site protection and management categories, with no consistent directional response across species. Sensitivity analyses restricted to the NE Poland detected no significant management associations after correction for multiple testing. Associations between site-level microhaplotype diversity and habitat characteristics also varied among species. Species traits showed suggestive associations with management-related changes in FHAP, although none remained statistically significant after correction for multiple-testing. Overall, microhaplotypes retain linked within-locus genetic variation and broadly recover SNP-based patterns of population differentiation, while associations between forest context and genetic variation remain strongly species-dependent.

items.title: Predicting antibiotic resistance evolution by mapping the local fitness landscape
items.blurb: Antibiotic resistance evolution is shaped by the distribution of fitness effects (DFE) of resistance mutations, yet measurements have been confined to small sets of mutants, single proteins, or knockout libraries. Here, we show that a map of the first mutational step toward chloramphenicol resistance in Escherichia coli makes subsequent evolution largely predictable. Using high-throughput barcoding, we collected more than 500 spontaneous resistant mutants and measured fitness across antibiotic concentrations. With increasing concentration, the DFE broadened and its beneficial tail changed from bounded to heavy, producing rare, exceptionally fit mutants. A dose--response scaling principle explains this pattern and predicts the fitness of each mutant at any concentration from just two mutant-specific parameters. Whole-genome sequencing linked these fitness effects to their underlying mutations, exposing a vast mutational target that is dominated by amplifications and loss-of-function mutations, reaches from efflux regulators to central metabolism, and contains variants of minimal fitness cost in every class. Population-genetic simulations built on these data, without any fitted parameters, predicted the phenotypic and mutational outcomes of longer-term evolution experiments. Mapping local fitness landscapes may thus offer a general route to forecasting antibiotic resistance evolution.

items.title: Organization of digestive functions in the chordate gut
items.blurb: Despite their widely different anatomies, the digestive tracts of all animals must perform a set of core functions that allow the animal to acquire and utilize nutrients from the environment. Whether there are general principles that govern how these functions are spatially organized, however, remains unclear. Here we show that the digestive tract of the tunicate Ciona robusta is organized into pigmented and unpigmented domains specialized for nutrient uptake and metabolism, respectively. We identify the major pigment as halocynthiaxanthin, a diet-derived carotenoid that accumulates in the vacuolated, microvilli-rich epithelium of the pigmented domains, marking the absorptive regions along the gut. We find a similar spatial separation of uptake and metabolism in a distantly related tunicate, Styela clava, despite a markedly different pigmentation pattern, as well as in the mouse small intestine along both the anterior-posterior and crypt-villus axes. These findings suggest that the spatial separation of uptake from metabolism is a conserved principle of chordate gut organization. We propose that the underlying trade-off between these two functions may have served as an organizing force in the evolution of specialized digestive cell types and organs.

items.title: Genomic insights into the evolutionary history and diversification of water voles (Arvicola spp.)
items.blurb: Water voles (Arvicola spp.) exhibit substantial morphological, ecological, and genetic variation which has initiated a longstanding debate over their evolutionary history and taxonomic status. Although five species have recently been proposed; ,A. amphibius, A. sapidus, A. persicus, A. italicus and A. monticola, their evolutionary relationships and divergence times remain poorly resolved. Here, we analyse 115 complete mitochondrial genomes and nuclear genomic data from 45 individuals representing all currently proposed species. We estimate that modern water voles began diverging ca. 400 ka ago, considerably more recently than previously estimated but broadly consistent with the fossil record. Further diversification occurred during the Middle and Late Pleistocene. However, we detect multiple discordances between the mitochondrial and nuclear relationships, and admixture analyses suggest that there has been historical gene flow between lineages. Furthermore, we find lower long-term effective population sizes and reduced genetic variation in several southern populations, potentially reflecting more restricted habitat availability or greater isolation than in central and northern populations. Additionally, in Georgia we identify a sister lineage to A. persicus and show that Anatolian water voles actually belong to this lineage and not A. amphibius . Our findings offer new insights into the complex evolutionary history of water voles, which was initially shaped by Pleistocene climatic fluctuations and subsequently reshaped by gene flow.

items.title: Transitory Invasion Graphs
items.blurb: Invasion graphs map community assembly by linking communities that contain stable equilibria through successful invasions. By design, they leave aside transient communities that arise when species arrive before a community settles. Transitory invasion graphs (TIGs) complement this framework by recording every observed community, stable or transient, weighted by its frequency. In 500 simulated competitive communities of 5 - 25 species, assembly expanded through many transient communities, then contracted onto a few attractors. Competition limited the expansion: stronger interactions produced fewer communities but more transitions among them. The contraction reflected the attractor type: stable-equilibrium communities settled on the endpoints predicted by invasion graphs, whereas cyclic and chaotic communities kept turning over, most often through communities away from those endpoints. Repeated invasion attempts also rescued species with negative invasion growth rates and occasionally displaced uninvadable equilibria. Together, invasion graphs and TIGs reveal both where assembly can end and what is observed along the way.

items.title: Quantifying and interpreting the inverse coefficient of variation from minirhizotron-derived root dynamics
items.blurb: 1. The inverse coefficient of variation (/{sigma}) is widely used to quantify temporal invariability of ecosystem functioning. However, most studies have focused on aboveground biomass production, while belowground processes remain understudied. Minirhizotrons enable repeated observations of root dynamics, but the resulting data differ fundamentally in their temporal structure from measurements obtained through aboveground biomass harvests, sequential soil coring, or ingrowth cores. This raises questions about whether inverse CV estimates depend on the metric used to represent root dynamics and on when and how frequently observations are made. 2. Using a five-year minirhizotron dataset, we quantified the inverse CV from standing root abundance and two change-based metrics (net change and rate of change in standing root abundance). Standing root abundance was quantified from individual imaging sessions, whereas change-based metrics were derived from differences between successive sessions. We compared their inverse CV estimates using all 45 imaging sessions, monthly observations (n = 35), and annual observations (n = 5). For annual observations, we compared measurements taken before the aboveground biomass harvest and at peak root abundance. 3. Inverse CV estimates differed between standing root abundance and change-based metrics, and correlations were weak and often negative. Estimates also differed across measurement frequencies and timings, with responses depending on the underlying metric. Together, these results show that inverse CV estimates depend on how root dynamics are represented and sampled. 4. We propose that the inverse CV does not always represent invariability and that its interpretation depends on the metric used to represent root dynamics. For standing root abundance, it reflects pool invariability. For change-based metrics, we suggest interpreting it as directional consistency of root gains or losses. This distinction may extend to other ecosystem fluxes that can be positive and negative, such as carbon or energy fluxes. 5. Synthesis. Our findings challenge the assumption that applying the same formula (/{sigma}) ensures comparability and emphasize the need to align the underlying ecological questions and quantities when comparing invariability across ecosystem realms or studies.

items.title: Resonance-organized phase-locking, extinction and phase-dependent rescue in periodically forced populations with delayed Allee effects
items.blurb: Population persistence under environmental fluctuations depends not only on the magnitude of external disturbances but also on their interaction with endogenous population dynamics. However, how environmental resonance interacts with delayed density dependence and Allee effects to determine extinction risk remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate a periodically forced Hutchinson-type population model incorporating delayed density regulation and a strong Allee effect. Through numerical simulations, Lyapunov exponent analysis, and bifurcation continuation, we characterize the organization of population dynamics and extinction across environmental forcing frequencies and amplitudes. We find that extinction vulnerability is strongly organized by resonance between endogenous population oscillations and environmental forcing, with the lowest forcing amplitudes required for extinction occurring near the principal 1:1 resonance. The parameter space exhibits a hierarchy of frequency-locking regions consistent with Arnold tongues, including structures bounded by saddle-node bifurcations of periodic orbits. We further demonstrate that the carrying-capacity-to-Allee-threshold ratio governs the emergence of intrinsic oscillations through a Hopf bifurcation, fundamentally reorganizing the population's response to environmental forcing. Counterintuitively, lowering the Allee threshold can increase extinction vulnerability by strengthening destabilizing delayed feedback. Finally, we identify a history-dependent rescue mechanism through which populations can recover after temporarily crossing below the nominal Allee threshold. Successful recovery events exhibit systematic phase dependence relative to environmental forcing. Together, these findings demonstrate that extinction risk cannot be inferred from environmental severity, population abundance, or dynamical regularity alone. Instead, persistence emerges from the interaction between environmental timescales, endogenous oscillations, and history-dependent opportunities for recovery.

items.title: Environmental drivers of abundance and later seasonal activity of a salt marsh mosquito
items.blurb: 1. Climate and environmental change are altering the seasonal dynamics of insects worldwide, yet long-term datasets remain scarce for mosquito vectors in temperate regions. Consequently, the environmental drivers and phenological responses of mosquito populations are still poorly resolved in northern Europe. 2. Here, we test whether the seasonal timing and abundance of a specialist coastal mosquito are jointly shaped by climatic and tidal drivers, and whether its activity period has extended over a 14-year monitoring record. 3. We analysed a 14-year dataset (2012-2025) of the salt marsh mosquito Aedes detritus - one of the most common saltmarsh mosquitoes in Europe - collected from four British coastal wetland sites. Weekly catch data from the full time series were used to assess long-term phenological trends, while generalised additive models were applied to site-month aggregated observations from the consistent four-site trapping period (2019-2025) to identify climatic and tidal drivers of abundance. 4. Across the full 14-year record, the late-season peak and the end of the activity period (the 90% activity week) shifted later by 0.52 and 0.76 weeks per year, respectively (equivalent to fitted shifts of approximately 7 and 10 weeks), with no corresponding advance in the spring onset. This delayed autumn activity was robust to sampling-window and moving-window controls. 5. Adult abundance showed a pronounced bimodal seasonal pattern, with a smaller peak in late spring and a larger peak in mid-autumn. After accounting for seasonal structure, rainfall at a one-month lag and tidal surge were both positively associated with mosquito abundance. The size of the spring peak was correlated with rainfall, but the size and timing of the autumn peak were not. 6. These findings provide evidence that the seasonal activity of a salt marsh mosquito is extending later into autumn. We show that its population dynamics reflects a combination of climatic and tidal drivers whose relative contributions will require longer or more finely resolved records to disentangle fully. Sustained, long-term, full-season monitoring of coastal mosquito populations would therefore be important for understanding their responses to climate change. We recommend extending mosquito sampling in salt marsh areas into late autumn to better assess future risks associated with mosquito-borne pathogens.

items.title: Reconciling multiple views of global marine plankton diversity
items.blurb: Marine plankton diversity influences key ecosystem properties, including primary production and carbon export, and is monitored using diverse observation systems. Yet, it remains unclear whether global diversity patterns from different observation streams converge, and whether potential commonalities can guide monitoring, modelling, and conservation. Using a habitat modelling (CEPHALOPOD), we compare plankton diversity patterns across observation types and metrics, relating global open-ocean surface diversity from 330,000 observations of occurrence, abundance, biomass, and relative metagenomic reads to environmental climatologies. We find that diversity patterns converge on a latitudinal diversity gradient, with tropical oligotrophic gyres, western boundary currents and the Info-Pacific archipelago emerging as diversity hotspots. Occurrence-based estimates indicate higher diversity in eastern boundary upwellings than estimates accounting for community dominance, showing how multiple observation types provide complementary views of diversity. Surface ocean temperature, primary production, and physical transport emerge as remotely observable diversity proxies that can guide in situ sampling. Finally, diversity-ecosystem functioning relationships depend on the observation system: occurrence-based estimates highlight how diverse species can support production through complementary ecological roles, whereas abundance-, biomass-, and metagenomic-based estimates better reflect how dominant species contribute to processes such as carbon export. These findings can guide monitoring, modelling, and conservation under climate change.

items.title: Using Mixture Density Networks to Predict Plot-level Environmental Factors from Tree Secondary Metabolites
items.blurb: Tropical forests contain remarkable phytochemical diversity, but the relationship between diverse plant metabolites and underlying climatic and environmental variation remains poorly understood. Mixture density networks (MDNs) offer a flexible approach for predicting variables with multimodal distributions. Traditional regression models produce single-value predictions, which may fail to capture the full variability of widely distributed variables. We evaluated the performance of an MDN model on a Panama metabolomics dataset, in which each metabolite occurs across multiple forest plots, resulting in environmental variables with multiple associated values. The MDN recovered the overall range and broad shape of environmental distributions, although feature-specific predictions often converged toward shared distributional patterns. These results suggest that mixture density networks can capture coarse environmental structure from metabolomic representations, while also highlighting challenges associated with limited environmental variation and sparse observations.

items.title: Coral monitoring with environmental DNA captures community restructuring after mass bleaching mortality
items.blurb: Marine heatwaves are restructuring coral reefs, but monitoring coral community change across impacted habitats and reefs remains expensive and logistically challenging. Metabarcoding of seawater DNA represents a potential solution to the issue of scale, but technical challenges and a lack of ground truthing with conventional measures of coral community structure have limited its application. In early 2025, Mermaid Reef in the Rowley Shoals, a remote oceanic atoll in northwest Australia, experienced unprecedented heat stress resulting in widespread coral bleaching and mortality. Using photo-transect data alongside seawater eDNA samples, we quantified changes in coral cover and community assemblage before and after the heatwave and compared results of the two monitoring methods. Photo-transect data showed sharp reductions in live coral cover, particularly in Acropora, the dominant pre-bleaching genus. eDNA data mirrored these shifts, and Acropora sequences dominated pre-bleaching samples but declined strongly after bleaching, while several less abundant genera increased in relative read abundance. Across sites and timepoints, eDNA reads corresponded to photo-transect cover, and multivariate assemblage patterns strongly aligned between the two methods. These results demonstrate that seawater eDNA metabarcoding can provide rapid detection of community restructuring on coral reefs and can augment existing monitoring frameworks.

items.title: Spectral tuning of proton-pumping rhodopsins underscores distinct light adaptations in polar diatoms
items.blurb: Resource limitation constrains primary production across vast regions of the global ocean. Diatoms often persist under these conditions, despite their relatively large size and nutrient quotas compared to other phytoplankton phyla. This trend is particularly pronounced in the variable light and iron-depleted waters of the Southern Ocean. Proton-pumping rhodopsins (PPRs) have emerged as an important adaptation underlying this success, allowing diatoms to energetically supplement chlorophyll-based photosynthesis with retinal-based phototrophy, particularly under iron stress. While PPRs are increasingly recognized as a driver of diatom resilience under iron depletion, the extent to which coinciding environmental factors, such as light, shape this adaptation remains unresolved. We performed an in vitro study to investigate how variations in iron availability and light spectra synergistically shape PPR physiology in two ecologically relevant Southern Ocean diatoms: Pseudo-nitzschia subcurvata and Synedra hyperborea. Integrative biochemical and bioinformatic approaches identified two distinct evolutionary strategies for rhodopsin-mediated light acquisition. While P. subcurvata employed a specialist approach with two PPRs utilized under different wavelengths of light (green v. blue/red), S. hyperborea adopted a generalist approach with expression of a single PPR under both light treatments. Structural analyses of PPRs revealed hallmarks consistent with xanthorhodopsins, while coordinated transcriptional and pigment analyses suggest the blue-absorbing xanthophyll diadinoxanthin functions as a secondary light-harvesting chromophore. Collectively, these findings expand the ecological light niche of diatom rhodopsins, reveal previously unrecognized diversity in eukaryotic rhodopsin strategies, and suggest spectral tuning of proton pumping rhodopsins will enhance diatom fitness within the climatically altered light climate of the Southern Ocean.

items.title: Out of the wild: lab-reared bumble bees lack environmental bacteria and fungi
items.blurb: Social bees, including bumble bees, host a community of microbes in their gut consisting of core bacterial taxa as well as non-core bacteria and fungi. Bumble bee research colonies from commercial suppliers are often utilized in research characterizing and examining the functions of bee microbiomes. However, commercial rearing conditions have the potential to shift the microbiome associated with bees, calling into question whether results obtained using commercial colonies are applicable to wild bees. Here, we examine differences between the microbiome of commercially-reared and wild caught bumble bees of three species (Bombus impatiens, B. terrestris, and B. vosnesenskii) using amplicon sequencing and qPCR to characterize bacterial and fungal communities within bee guts. We found that while all bee species hosted some microbes belonging to the core bumble bee gut community, microbial community composition and diversity varied between species and sources, with wild individuals lacking some groups of core bacteria and hosting a greater diversity of non-core bacterial and fungal taxa. This work highlights the presence and potential dominance of non-core microbial taxa within wild bumble bee gut communities, especially early in the colony life cycle. Overall, we conclude that rearing conditions can shape the composition of bumble bee microbiomes, and research on commercial colonies alone may overlook environmental taxa commonly associated with bees.

items.title: Trade-off between resource excretion and reliance maintains biodiversity of a cross-feeding mutualism
items.blurb: Microbial mutualisms, in which species exchange resources through cross-feeding, are common in nature. Yet the stability of mutualistic interactions is debated, and cross-feeding communities are vulnerable to cheaters that benefit from the excretions of others but reduce or cease their own excretion of resources, which can lead to community collapse. Here, we demonstrate with a mathematical model that in addition to decreased excretion, increased reliance on cross-fed resources can also lead to community collapse. In a two-species model of bacteria that metabolizes lactose and provides yeast with galactose, in exchange for amino acids from yeast, we show that the set of excretion and reliance parameters that maximizes biomass is adjacent to a region of community collapse in the phase diagram. By expanding the model to include multiple bacterial auxotrophs competing for lactose and either separate or overlapping amino acids, we also demonstrate that a trade-off between reliance and excretion can enable coexistence within the bacterial mutualist guild. Finally, we show that intraguild coexistence of bacteria favors yeast, increasing biodiversity but decreasing total community biomass. Our results argue that the question of cheaters should be paired with analysis of reliance on mutualistic exchange, and that both of these parameters modulate biodiversity and the stability of mutualisms to collapse.

items.title: Sodium-enriched nectar increases seed set in low diversity prairies
items.blurb: Plant-pollinator interactions depend on floral traits and background plant community properties, yet the role of nectar micronutrients in these interactions is poorly understood. Sodium is a micronutrient of particular interest because although plants need little to no sodium, animal pollinators require it. It is unknown whether sodium-enriched nectar increases plant fitness in animal-pollinated plants and how this may be affected by the broader plant community. To test this, we grew black-eyed Susan (Rudbeckia hirta) plants in sodium-enriched or control soil. We placed pairs of sodium-addition and control plants in prairies seeded with high or low diversity and measured seed set and germination rate. In a supplementary experiment, we explored differences in floral visitation. We found that black-eyed Susan plants grown in sodium-enriched soil had sodium-enriched nectar. Seed set increased in sodium-addition plants in prairies seeded with low diversity but not in prairies seeded with high diversity. Germination rate was not affected by sodium addition. Altogether, our study highlights the importance of considering both micronutrients and context dependency in understanding plant reproduction and complex species interactions.

items.title: Belowground Herbivory Shapes Carbon Release from Tree Roots and Its Retention in Soil
items.blurb: Belowground root inputs contribute to stable soil organic carbon (SOC) significantly more than aboveground plant inputs. Yet, current understanding of the role of belowground root herbivory in ecosystem C cycling is remarkably weaker than that of aboveground herbivory and litter inputs. Here, we experimentally exposed roots of co-occurring mature hickory (Carya) and maple (Acer) trees, in a temperate hardwood forest, to increasing herbivory pressure by ubiquitous root-feeding soil nematodes. We investigated responses and underlying mechanisms of root C exudation as well as downstream indirect effects of root herbivory on mineral-associated organic carbon (MAOC) pools. Increased root herbivory promoted C exudation, which was strongly associated with increasing root necrosis and resulted in indirect positive effects on MAOC. Importantly, these direct and indirect effects were larger in magnitude and only significant in hickory but not maple. Instead, the latter appeared to channel herbivory response toward diversified chemical defense signaling rather than bulk exudate release, while more extensive root damage and increased exudation rate with less compositional change of hickory suggested a greater role of passive exudate release through leaking wounds in roots. Taken together, these findings indicate divergent eco-physiological mechanisms and ecosystem C consequences of root herbivory in mature hickory and maple trees, and show that changes in exudate quantity rather than chemical composition impact soil C. This study extends field-based causal explanation of root C inputs and retention in soil by highlighting the role of root-feeding animals in regulating rhizodeposition, and offers a basis for integrating belowground herbivory into multitrophic biogeochemistry.

items.title: Scientists discover a surprising twist in how the body burns calories
items.blurb: Researchers have discovered that a drug can significantly increase the body's energy expenditure without clearly activating calorie-burning brown fat. The unexpected finding reveals a new challenge in developing obesity treatments that harness the body's natural fat-burning machinery.

items.title: Minecraft-like DNA cubes self-assemble into complex 3D nanostructures
items.blurb: Associate professor Petr Sulc and his research team have developed a programmable DNA-based building system that could open new possibilities for nanorobots, three-dimensional electronics and next-generation nanotechnology.

items.title: Artificial photosynthesis uses waste CO₂ to grow protein-rich edible fungus in seven days
items.blurb: While many people think first of meat when they think about dietary protein, most protein ultimately depends on plants, since livestock feed on grass, hay and other plants. Meeting the demand for protein is taxing on the environment, requiring massive amounts of land and water while creating greenhouse gas emissions. And that demand is expected to require nearly 50% more agricultural production by 2050 than in 2012, according to the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organization.

items.title: Draining peatlands leaves a long legacy of warming
items.blurb: Peatland ecosystems like bogs and swamps perform an important balancing act: Their vegetation takes up huge amounts of carbon dioxide, while their soil microbes produce methane. Although methane is a potent greenhouse gas, peatlands exhibit a net cooling effect on the planet because of the sheer scale of carbon dioxide they remove from the atmosphere, which has amounted to hundreds of gigatons globally over thousands of years.

items.title: Stabilizing atomically thin metals with sandwich structures: Machine learning expands the search
items.blurb: Atomically thin metals, metallenes, are promising materials for catalysis, electronics and energy conversion, but their synthesis has been challenging. Researchers from the University of Jyväskylä have now identified more than 300 stable metallene sandwich structures using machine learning and high-performance computing. The results provide researchers with a practical roadmap for the fabrication of new two-dimensional metals.

items.title: Smartphone app uses AI to identify illegal wildlife products
items.blurb: Illegal and unsustainable wildlife trade is a major driver of biodiversity loss. Thousands of animal species are traded, along with products made from them, ranging from ivory to scales and powders.

items.title: Certain fungi turn specialized plant cells into water-carrying cells using one protein
items.blurb: Can a pathogen that causes damage to a plant also make that plant more resilient to drought? An international research team led by the University of Göttingen has investigated this apparent paradox. The researchers discovered how certain fungi promote the formation of new water-conducting cells in plants. At the same time, infected plants showed increased tolerance to drought stress. The results were published in the journal Cell Host & Microbe.

items.title: Carbon nanotube measurements reveal quantum model better explains collective electron behavior
items.blurb: An international team of scientists from Lithuania, Finland and Israel has conducted both theoretical and experimental research into carbon nanotubes, becoming the first to demonstrate which physical model governs the motion and interactions of electrons within them.

items.title: Five reasons why we should still make things with our hands
items.blurb: It's 7 a.m. Still dark outside. "Alex, time to wake up! You have a busy day ahead, with an important meeting at 8:30," announces the alarm in a soft but firm voice. Alex wakes up immediately, already thinking about the presentation that still needs a few finishing touches. In the kitchen, the coffee machine, set up for 7 a.m. sharp, has just finished brewing. "Alexa, set the temperature to 20 degrees," says Alex, reaching for the coffee.

items.title: The Scientist Who Wants to Save Cranberries
items.blurb: A conversation with a Salk Institute plant genomicist, and cranberry fanatic, on his research into improving the fate of the Thanksgiving staple

items.title: New inhibitor restores antibiotic activity against drug-resistant bacteria
items.blurb: Researchers from Imperial College London and collaborators have identified a potent small-molecule inhibitor that can restore the activity of the antibiotic ciprofloxacin against methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA).

items.title: NASA's Europa Clipper zooming by Earth on way to Jupiter's icy moon
items.blurb: NASA's Europa Clipper will soon swing past Earth before making a yearslong beeline for Jupiter, where the orbiter will probe whether the ocean beneath its moon Europa's icy shell has the ingredients for life. The flyby will offer a propellant-saving boost and an opportunity to prepare for the science-gathering that lies ahead.

items.title: Shopping as a 'collector' makes us want to buy more, new research shows
items.blurb: Shoppers are more likely to buy products and pay more for them when they adopt a "collecting mindset," according to new research co-authored by Bayes Business School (City St George's, University of London).

items.title: Giant lambda-shaped stellar nursery found in the Milky Way's outskirts
items.blurb: Massive stars often form in dense regions, called "hubs," where filamentary structures made of star-forming materials meet. These star-forming complexes are "hub-filament" systems. Astronomers have discovered one such large network of molecular gas filaments in the outer regions of the Milky Way. It is called the λ-complex, and the structure is bigger than most known hub-filament systems. The research paper was published in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society on Nov. 17.

items.title: Sustainable procurement in multinational corporations depends on people and the operating environment
items.blurb: Elizabeth Jeromaa's doctoral dissertation in management, to be examined at the University of Vaasa, demonstrates that it is possible for companies to implement environmentally sustainable procurement practices, though there is no one-size-fits-all model.

items.title: Heaven scent: Study shows link between a partner's body odor and sexual intimacy
items.blurb: Many people spend a considerable amount of time and money trying to disguise their natural body odor. But not everyone finds our natural scent unpleasant. In fact, it could be part of what makes a couple click.

items.title: Can Personality Traits Predict Who Stays Single?
items.blurb: Singlehood is more complicated than you might think

items.title: Using lunar craters as free radiation shields for moon base nuclear reactors
items.blurb: Powering any future lunar base is a massive engineering challenge. The two-week lunar night can drain batteries charged by solar panels during the two-week day, if the batteries themselves can even withstand the freezing temperatures that go along with it. So, for decades at this point, engineers have planned to use a nuclear reactor to at least partially power any future human settlement on the moon.

items.title: Simulations reveal how a solar vortex and reconnecting magnetic fields can launch a rotating jet
items.blurb: Solar spicules are slender jets commonly found in the chromosphere. They lift relatively cool plasma from the lower solar atmosphere, carry energy upward, and in some cases rotate as they evolve. Small-scale vortices also occur frequently between convection-driven granules in the photosphere. Two questions remain incompletely answered: how these photospheric vortices help form spicules, and how much mass and energy the rising jets carry into the corona.

items.title: Without marine life, atmospheric CO₂ would shoot up by up to 65% by the end of the century
items.blurb: Without marine organisms transporting carbon into the deep ocean, the accumulation of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere would be drastically higher in the year 2100, reaching levels between 35% and 65% higher than projected. This is one of the main conclusions of the new policy brief developed within the framework of the European OceanICU project, which was presented at the United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Türkiye.

items.title: Structural agility of 2D crystals enables digital doping of graphene superlattices
items.blurb: A study published in Nature has demonstrated that applying an electric field can switch the atomic arrangement in a stack of two-dimensional (2D) crystals, accompanied by an unusual charge behavior. This provides a new experimental platform for exploring how the structural and electronic properties of atomically thin materials interact.

items.title: Uterine pressure guides head-to-tail axis formation in mouse embryos
items.blurb: During animal development, the establishment of the three primary body axes—head-to-tail (anterior-posterior), dorsal-ventral and left-right—is essential for building a proper body structure. A fertilized egg, initially a single cell, undergoes repeated cell divisions to form a multicellular structure called an embryo, and body axes are formed within the embryo.

items.title: Weak oversight and financial incentives may fuel health care corruption, review finds
items.blurb: Corruption in health systems may arise when governance failures offer opportunities and systemic vulnerabilities provide incentives for private gain, according to an umbrella review published in the open-access journal PLOS Global Public Health by Michele Coleman and Petra Varkonyi from the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, United Kingdom, and colleagues.

items.title: The triple helix: How a rare twist in human evolution may influence fetal cooling
items.blurb: The human umbilical cord is an evolutionary rarity, with the arrangement of blood vessels within its distinctive twisted structure potentially helping unborn babies stay cool in the womb, according to a team led by University of Manchester and University of Southampton scientists.

items.title: Mapping the uncharted plate tectonic cycle: The hidden path from plate destruction to new oceanic crust
items.blurb: Since the discovery of plate tectonics, the ultimate fate of the massive plates that sink into Earth's interior mantle at subduction zones has remained a major geological quest. Meanwhile, magma continuously rises from the deep mantle to form new oceanic crust, erupting as mid-ocean ridge basalts (MORB).

items.title: New England's summer thunderstorms grow shorter and heavier, raising flash flood risk
items.blurb: A growing share of New England's summer rain is falling in the form of heavy, heat-related showers and thunderstorms, raising the risk of flash flooding events across the region as the climate continues to warm. That's according to a new study by Brown University researchers published in Science Advances.

items.title: Errors in judging friendships predict who will connect or drift apart six months later
items.blurb: Decades of research show that mental representations of social networks are riddled with errors, with people commonly misidentifying existing ties and reporting relationships that do not exist. While these inaccuracies have been interpreted as noise arising from the limits of memory or attention, Brown University researchers have discovered a much more intriguing explanation: These "errors" are accurate representations of social connections that just haven't happened yet.

items.title: Evolution's balancing act—keeping genes in sync after genome duplication
items.blurb: Getting the right balance is important in all walks of life, whether it's a healthy combination of food groups in a balanced diet or a balanced mix of skills that allows a work or sports team to succeed.

items.title: Seabird ‘spies’ could help spot ships that aren’t broadcasting their location
items.blurb: Researchers have found that seabirds equipped with audio recorders and GPS trackers can detect ships, offering a way to monitor fishing vessels that are operating illegally

items.title: This Newly Discovered Whale Species Had a Lopsided Skull
items.blurb: Not the most aesthetically pleasing look, but essential for survival

items.title: AI’s stunning progress in maths shows how little we understand it
items.blurb: The biggest problem in maths has been cracked by AI, but it remains impossible to predict how its capabilities will advance in other fields

Is The Time Traveler’s Wife the perfect audiobook to experience on shuffle?

items.blurb: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03854-x The biggest problem in mathematics has to do with a statistical test familiar to scientists.

items.blurb: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03494-1 Chromosome-scale genome sequences from across the barley genus Hordeum reveal large structural variation, evidence of ancient genetic exchange and extensive divergence of regulatory sequences. These evolutionary processes have generated diversity that could be used to improve cultivated barley.

items.title: Pockets in compacted DNA tune gene activation
items.blurb: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03492-3 The stochastic activation of specific genes is needed for the proper formation of neuronal circuits. Opposing forces act on inactive DNA to balance this process.

items.title: Bogong moths can migrate using an internal geomagnetic compass
items.blurb: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03693-w Australian migratory moths navigate long distances, in part owing to a stellar ‘compass’. It transpires that they have another compass that detects the inclination, or angle, of Earth’s magnetic field lines and that probably relies on a light-dependent quantum-mechanical mechanism similar to the one found in night-migratory songbirds.

items.blurb: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11315-8 In flies, sugar-sensing enteric neurons activate brain neurons that inhibit crop duct motor neurons, relaxing the foregut muscles to facilitate food transfer to the crop, which sustains ingestion and regulates food intake.

items.title: Disturbances and climate drive tree elevational shifts
items.blurb: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11354-1 Climate change and natural disturbances are key drivers of tree abundance dynamics: warming tends to shift tree abundance upslope whereas major disturbances, such as wildfires and insect outbreaks, tend to shift it downslope, creating opposing pressures on tree species’ elevational redistribution.

items.title: Unconventional resistivity reduction in NbP semimetal nanoribbons
items.blurb: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11288-8 Niobium phosphide semimetal nanoribbons show decreasing resistivity with decreasing width, unlike the classical behaviour of metals such as copper, offering a platform for nanoscale wires and interconnects via industry-friendly top-down nanofabrication.

items.title: De novo design of high-potency dual-target therapeutic peptides with ORIDTP
items.blurb: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11338-1 The artificial intelligence platform ORIDTP enabled de novo design of potent dual-target therapeutic peptides, generating candidate anti-obesity, antidiabetic and anticancer peptides with strong in vivo efficacy and broad cross-target generalizability.

items.title: Engineering signalling centres to trigger human trunk morphogenesis in vitro
items.blurb: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11326-5 A high-throughput synthetic embryology platform reveals how transient spatial cues establish two self-sustaining signalling centres that organize trunk-like morphogenesis, enabling the study of early human development and congenital disorders.

items.title: Rare-variant genetic architecture of height in over 1.4 million individuals
items.blurb: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11345-2 Analysis of exomes from over 1.4 million participants implicates 207 genes, including large effect coding variants and gene burden tests, and demonstrates the utility of large-scale sequencing for trait prediction and variant interpretation.

items.title: Submillimetre hot-electron transport in manganese-doped quantum dot solids
items.blurb: Nature, Published online: 25 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11279-9 A phototransport regime driven by spin exchange is demonstrated in manganese-doped quantum dot solids, enabling the generation, long-range transport and regeneration of hot carriers and yielding submillimetre drift lengths.

items.title: ceTDP: A Practical Tutorial on Valid and Quantitative Cluster-Extent Inference in Neuroimaging
items.blurb: We introduce ceTDP, a two-stage framework for cluster-extent inference in neuroimaging that extends conventional random field theory-based and permutation-based methods. In contrast to standard cluster inference, which yields binary significance, ceTDP additionally quantifies the proportion of truly active voxels within clusters using the true discovery proportion (TDP). The method is built on closed testing and provides strong family-wise error rate control while remaining consistent with standard cluster inference. The framework operates in two stages: estimation of a cluster-extent threshold, followed by computation of the TDP lower bound. Two complementary procedures are provided: a conservative, statistically guaranteed TDP lower bound (ceTDP-cons) and a heuristic approach for obtaining a potentially tighter estimate of the TDP lower bound (ceTDP-heur). Together, they enable both rigorous inference and improved sensitivity in cluster-level analysis.

items.title: A comprehensive Drosophila toolkit reveals context-dependent functional hierarchies across RasG12X variants in vivo
items.blurb: KRAS is a GTPase regulating key signalling processes involved in cell proliferation, differentiation, growth and survival. KRAS is the most prevalent oncogene in human cancers, often acquiring a point mutation at Glycine 12 (G12). Although several possible amino acid substitutions occur at this hotspot in humans, most animal cancer models often examine only a single or limited subset of G12X variants, restricting our understanding of their distinct biological effects. Here, we describe a novel transgenic toolkit in Drosophila melanogaster comparing the most frequently observed oncogenic G12X variants (G12A, G12C, G12D, G12R, G12S, G12V), and evaluate these across multiple developmental and tumour contexts in vivo. Interestingly, we demonstrate how the phenotypic strength of each G12X variant differs significantly depending on the biological context, highlighting the importance of considering these point mutations systematically. Overall, our comprehensive RasG12X toolkit provides a powerful and versatile platform to explore the dysregulation of KRAS in vivo, serving as a valuable resource enabling unprecedented opportunities to investigate variant- and context-specific mechanisms of oncogenic signalling with direct relevance to cancer biology and therapy.

items.title: An isogenic platform to model the impact of sex chromosome and donor genotype in hiPSC-derived vascular smooth muscle cells
items.blurb: Monosomy-X results in Turner Syndrome (TS), which beyond its cardinal height and reproductive phenotypes, spans incompletely penetrant cardiovascular phenotypes, including bicuspid valve, hypoplastic left-sided heart syndrome and aortic coarctation. These congenital heart defects (CHD) conspire with hypertension to dilate the ascending aorta, which can progress to rupture and drive early mortality in TS. Genetic contributors to incompletely penetrant phenotypes in TS remain only partially explored, thus complicating risk stratification. To begin addressing this challenge in donor-specific in-vitro models, we derived monosomy-X human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) alongside isogenic euploid control lines from donors mosaic for the second sex chromosome. In embryonic-origin specific vascular smooth muscle cells (vSMCs) derived from these hiPSCs, monosomy-X reveals donor-specific cellular and transcriptomic effects, with expression changes in one donor panel enriched in genes previously implicated in coronary artery disease and ascending aorta diameter. Polygenic risk scores (PGS) for cardiovascular traits mirror this transcriptomic enrichment, and suggest PGS analysis may help to prioritize hiPSC lines for in-vitro modeling of incompletely-penetrant traits related to TS-associated aortopathy.

items.title: Genetically Encoded Photodecaging of Asparagine Enables Protein Function Control and Time-Resolved N-Glycosylation
items.blurb: Asparagine contributes to protein function through its polar carboxamide side chain and serves as the acceptor residue for N-linked glycosylation, yet temporally controlling these roles directly through the side-chain carboxamide remains challenging. Here, we report the genetic encoding of N4-(2-nitrobenzyl)-L-asparagine (ONBN), a photocaged asparagine that regenerates the native side-chain carboxamide upon 365 nm irradiation. Engineered aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase/tRNA pairs enabled site-specific ONBN incorporation into proteins in Escherichia coli and mammalian cells. Photodecaging restored Renilla luciferase activity and activated TRAF6 polyubiquitination mediated by UBE2N in living cells. Beyond active-site residues, we further developed CAGE-proxN, using computationally guided proximal caging to optically activate firefly luciferase. Finally, ONBN incorporation at the acceptor position of an N-glycosylation sequon enabled light-triggered initiation and time-resolved monitoring of post-translational glycan installation on an endoplasmic reticulum-targeted reporter. Variation of the -2 flanking residue revealed sequence-dependent differences in apparent glycosylation kinetics. This work extends genetically encoded photocontrol to the asparagine carboxamide and provides a platform for investigating asparagine-dependent protein functions and the temporal regulation of N-glycosylation in living cells.

items.title: Self-generated action shapes theta phase alignment at encoding and later recollection
items.blurb: Across species, self-directed action is linked to theta rhythms and better memory, but such action combines choosing, moving, and controlling the outcome. Whether choosing and control over the outcome shape recollection, and the encoding dynamics that support it, remains unclear. Three preregistered experiments in human participants separated these components while holding movement constant. Participants encoded scene pairs by dragging either a freely chosen scene or one indicated by the program, with fluent or disrupted feedback. Recognition was tested after 24 hours (and immediately in Experiment 2), using Remember/Know judgments. Experiment 3 recorded scalp electroencephalography during encoding. Choosing improved recognition, more for recollection than familiarity. A smaller benefit extended to the unselected scene, although less consistently after latency adjustment. Disrupted feedback lowered rated agency but did not reduce memory at 24 hours. In Experiment 2, however, recollection declined less over 24 hours after self-generated than externally generated action, but only under fluent feedback. Choosing increased action-onset-locked theta and alpha phase alignment (inter-trial phase coherence), whereas disrupted feedback reduced alignment later. The selection effects survived matching for response-initiation-latency. Trial by trial, later posterior theta alignment (353-570 ms) predicted Remember over Know responses, whereas early frontal alpha alignment (127-245 ms) predicted Remember over Forgotten responses.
