items.title: Guatemala: El Niño drought pushes families to sell possessions or send children to work to afford food
items.blurb:
Country: Guatemala
Source: Save the Children

GUATEMALA CITY, 26 November 2026 -- Families in Guatemala are resorting to desperate measures to stave off hunger as the El Niño-induced drought gripping the country worsens such as selling their possessions or sending children to work, said Save the Children.

Almost half (47%) of over 3,330 families surveyed by Save the Children in August in El Quiché, a critical agriculture hub in the northwestern highlands, reported losing their harvests during the last year, [1]. This has left many farming-dependent families at risk of hunger as the country’s food security situation continues to deteriorate according to data released this month.[2]

Four in 10 families told Save the Children that the drought was the reason for the loss of their harvests - reflective of a broader trend across Central America. [3] Since the survey in August, the El Niño weather phenomenon has strengthened in the country and is expected to continue well into 2027.

Four in five (79%) families supported by Save the Children depend on wages from seasonal daily farm labour and this loss is driving families to resort to increasingly desperate coping mechanisms. About 42% of families in drought-affected areas said they were forced to sell household assets or possessions to generate income.

Some parents have been left with no choice but to migrate in search of seasonal work, leaving their children for months at a time with older children having to take care of younger siblings. Other families are borrowing maize or money from neighbours, leaving them in debt.

One in 10 households in communities supported by Save the Children also said that at least one child was out of school as families were unable to cover education costs such as books and transport or have been forced to send children to work.

Rosa,* a 28-year-old mother from El Quiché supported by Save the Children, said: “Nothing came from the harvest. Everything was lost. We did our part and planted our crops, but we got nothing in return. Most families here in the community were unable to harvest anything from what they planted.”

According to the leading global hunger monitor, the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC), almost one in five (18%) people in Guatemala do not know where their next meal will come from - more than initially projected.[4] The country also has one of the world’s highest stunting rates, with 47% of children under five too short for their height.[5]

Moa Cortobius, Save the Children’s climate resilience adviser for Latin America and the Caribbean, said:

“The devastating drought in Guatemala is pushing already vulnerable farming families to the brink, destroying crops and disrupting livelihoods, making it harder for parents to put food on the table for their children.

“Hunger is not just about missing meals. Children who do not have enough nutritious food are more likely to become malnourished, fall ill, miss school and face increased risks of exploitation and abuse – trapping children and families in a cycle it can be difficult to escape from without support. We are seeing families forced to make difficult decisions such as taking children out of school or sending them to work just so the family has enough to eat.

“El Niño is wreaking havoc in Guatemala, a country already facing a significant child nutrition crisis. We know that anticipatory action works, and we know which are the most vulnerable children. By protecting children and families before the drought becomes a crisis, we can avoid the worst impacts on children, save lives and protect essential services like schools, hospitals, and water supply."

While El Niño is a naturally occurring phenomenon, human-induced climate change has amplified its threat.

Save the Children is calling on governments, donors and civil society to act decisively on information from early warning systems now, before more lives and livelihoods are lost.

Save the Children has worked in Guatemala since 1976 and supported 150,000 people in 2025. The organisation is supporting families affected by the drought in El Quiché with cash assistance to help families purchase food, hygiene promotion, distribution of household water filters, protection and psychosocial support activities.

Save the Children is also working to help at least one million people, including 600,000 children across 25 countries to prepare for El Niño by teaching children how to stay safe, sharing early warning information, keeping essential services running and supporting families with cash and livelihood assistance before disaster strikes.

Notes

[1] Informe Monitoreo, August 2026. The data was collected as part of regular aid distribution monitoring. Save the Children surveyed 3,334 families in four areas of El Quiché (comprising 21,231 people, including 8,237 children).

[2] GUATEMALA: Acute Food Insecurity Situation Update for October 2026 - February 2027. The update published in November revises the IPC’s earlier projection for the period October 2026 to February 2027 across the whole country, indicating a deterioration throughout the projection period.

https://www.ipcinfo.org/ipc-country-analysis/details-map/en/c/1165491/?iso3=Ge

[3] FAO data confirms a broader trend of harvest loss across the Central American region: El Niño 2026-2027: Riesgo climático y perspectiva humanitaria para América Latina y el Caribe al 18 de septiembre 2026 - Guatemala | ReliefWeb

[4] GUATEMALA: Acute Food Insecurity Situation Update for October 2026 - February 2027

[5] https://globalnutritionreport.org/resources/nutrition-profiles/latin-america-and-caribbean/central-america/guatemala/

items.title: Japan and World Food Programme Partner to Provide Nutritious School Meals for 50,000 Young Children in Lesotho
items.blurb:
Countries: Lesotho, Japan
Source: World Food Programme

MASERU, Lesotho – The United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) welcomes a JPY 200 million contribution, equivalent to USD 1.2 million, from the Government of Japan to provide nutritious school meals to 50,000 children in early childhood care and development centres across Lesotho.

The contribution comes as malnutrition remains a serious concern in Lesotho, where 36 percent of children under 5 are stunted. School meals provide a vital safety net for young children, particularly in rural communities, while supporting healthier diets, regular attendance and learning.

Speaking at a ceremony to announce the contribution, His Excellency Shimizu Fumio, Ambassador of Japan to Lesotho said: “For a child, a meal is about far more than simply addressing hunger. It provides the energy to learn, the nourishment to grow, and the opportunity to fully participate in school and in the community. By supporting children, we help build a healthier, stronger, and more capable future generation in Lesotho.”

The funding will enable WFP to purchase 430 mt of locally sourced fortified maize meal and pulses, as well as 81 mt of canned fish, improving the quality and diversity of school meals. These foods will complement the fortified porridge provided by the Government of Lesotho.

“A nutritious meal can make a lasting difference in a young child’s life,” said Anna Mukiibi-Bunnya, WFP Representative and Country Director in Lesotho. “With Japan’s generous support, thousands of children across Lesotho will have a stronger start in life and a better chance to fulfil their potential.”

WFP and the Government of Lesotho currently provide two meals each day to 50,000 children aged 2 to 5 years in 2,400 early childhood care and development centres. More than 80 percent of WFP-supported centres report high attendance, while 94 percent report that school meals contribute to improved learning.

Since 2019, the Government of Japan has contributed USD 15.7 million to support school meals and livelihood programmes implemented by the Government of Lesotho and WFP.

items.title: What we carried, what we left behind: Five accounts of displacement in Yemen
items.blurb:
Country: Yemen
Source: Danish Refugee Council

Please refer to the attached file.

Executive summary

When fighting forces a family to leave, there may be little time to decide what belongings to take with them, not knowing when – or if – they can return for the rest. Displacement uproots lives, stripping families of a sense of normality, comfort and home. People gather what they can carry and what they believe they will need. Behind them remain homes, possessions and often the means to earn a living.

Since August, more than 281,000 people have been displaced in Yemen*. Renewed hostilities are adding to existing needs that have accumulated over more than a decade of conflict. Families are seeking safety in displacement sites and host communities where shelter, water, sanitation and assistance are already stretched.

This document outlines accounts of five internally displaced persons (IDPs) describing what they brought, what they left behind and how their lives have changed since the increase in hostilities. Their priorities are personal and practical: continuing treatment, returning to school, finding work, having somewhere to cook and keeping their children warm.

Shelter and cash assistance from the Danish Refugee Council (DRC) has helped several of these families address immediate needs after arriving in Lahj. Their accounts also show what remains unresolved: bedding, cooking facilities, safe water, sanitation, continued treatment, education and income. DRC has worked in Yemen since 2008.

As of 3 November 2026 , its emergency reporting recorded assistance reaching more than 9,000 people in Lahj, including shelter and water, sanitation and hygiene(WASH) support and Multipurpose Cash Assistance (MPCA). DRC is also providing protection support and assessing barriers to services and assistance. Working with communities and partners, DRC identifies needs, coordinates services and supports newly displaced households alongside people living in prolonged displacement and vulnerable host communities.

Additional funding is urgently needed to expand this response. Redirecting existing resources can address an immediate gap, but risks reducing or delaying support elsewhere.

items.title: Sudan: Site Profile - Tawila Camp: North Darfur Humanitarian Response (15 November, 2026)
items.blurb:
Country: Sudan
Source: Norwegian Refugee Council

Please refer to the attached Infographic.

Operational Context & Approach

Since September 2026, Tawila has experienced successive waves of displacement, primarily from areas around Al Fasher, driven by severe food and resource shortages following poor rainfall, compounded by farmer–nomad tensions. As of 12 November 2026, 3,441 newly arrived HHs had been recorded. Arrivals initially concentrated in the Camp A - expansion area (Al-Omda, Abnagour), adding pressure to overstretched services. Phased relocations to Tina began on 17 October 2026; 3,044 HHs from the recent displacement wave were reported to have relocated. These arrivals are tracked separately from the population baseline of the five established camps.

Displacement continues across multiple locations. In Sharq Rwanda, the 1–2 November assessment identified 315 newly displaced HHs (1,585 people), with later operational updates indicating around 900 HHs. Tarni/Ajaj remains a proposed relocation area.

Reception capacity, shelter, food, water, sanitation, health and protection needs remain acute for newly arrived and relocated families, alongside unmet needs in the established camps.

While acknowledging the broader displacement situation and ongoing new arrivals, this Site Profile focuses on the five largest camps in Tawila, covering their population, service availability and priority needs and gaps.

items.title: Syria: Explosive Ordnance Knowledge, Attitudes and Practices survey in Aleppo governorate - Analysis and recommendations for Risk Education
items.blurb:
Country: Syrian Arab Republic
Source: HAMAP Humanitaire

Please refer to the attached file.

Executive summary

Safe Land and HAMAP-Humanitaire conducted this Knowledge, Attitudes and Practices (KAP) survey to better understand how communities in Aleppo Governorate perceive and respond to the threat of explosive ordnance (EO), and to ensure that future Explosive Ordnance Risk Education (EORE) activities are evidence-based and adapted to local realities. Data collection took place across eight target locations: Castello, Youth Housing, Khan Al-Asal, Maqbala, Al-Rashedin, Al-Mallah, Haritan and Ratyan.

Findings confirm that EO contamination remains a major humanitarian and socio-economic challenge in Aleppo. 82% of respondents reported avoiding certain areas because of EO hazards, while 62% had personally seen or encountered an explosive device and 74% knew someone who had been injured or killed by EO. Exposure is particularly acute in agricultural areas, where contamination continues to restrict access to farmland, grazing land and livelihoods.

Although awareness of contamination is widespread, important knowledge and behaviour gaps persist. While 91% of respondents had heard about mines or explosive remnants of war in their area, only 49% reported being able to identify a suspicious item, with significant disparities between men (63%) and women (33%). Unsafe reactions remain common: 1/3 of respondents would ignore a suspicious object, 15% reported they would handle or move it, and only 32% would report it to the authorities. In the event of an EO accident, most respondents would rush directly to assist the victim, potentially exposing themselves to secondary hazards.

The survey revealed a strong demand for risk education. 94% of respondents considered EORE important, while local NGOs (58%) and national authorities (52%) were identified as the most trusted actors to deliver awareness activities. Schools emerged as the preferred awareness channel, followed by community workshops, door-to-door outreach and digital platforms. Based on the findings, Maqbala, Al-Mallah and Youth Housing should be prioritised for future EORE interventions. Particular attention should be given to adult men aged 31-50, who display some of the highest levels of risky behaviour, and to adult women who demonstrated a lack of knowledge compared to men; while maintaining targeted outreach for children, adolescents, returnees and farming communities. Expanding school-based programming, strengthening digital outreach through WhatsApp and Facebook, increasing community and household engagement, and mobilising religious and community leaders will be critical to reducing EO-related risks and supporting safe recovery in Aleppo Governorate.

This KAP survey report was done jointly by Safe Land organisation and HAMAP-Humanitaire, with the special contributions of Nedal Shaheen, Bérengère Lenoir and Adèle Masson. The two organisations would like to thank all enumerators for their professionalism in conducting the data collection, all participants for their engagement in the survey and contributors in the report writing.

items.title: UNHCR Regional Response to the Yemen Situation One Month Impact Report-October 2026
items.blurb:
Countries: Yemen, Djibouti, Somalia
Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees

Please refer to the attached file.

Overview

Following a dramatic escalation of hostilities along Yemen’s western coast in September 2026, the humanitarian situation in the country has deteriorated rapidly. The surge in violence is compounding more than a decade of protracted conflict, widespread economic disruption, and collapsing public infrastructure. In direct response to the scale and velocity of the unfolding crisis, UNHCR declared a Level 1 Emergency for Yemen, Djibouti, and Somalia to scale up its preparedness and response efforts for an initial three-month duration.

Within the first 30 days of this emergency declaration, more than 250,000 individuals were newly internally displaced within Yemen, while thousands more undertook hazardous maritime journeys across the Bab el-Mandeb Strait to reach Djibouti, with hundreds also arriving in Somalia.

In Yemen, UNHCR has rapidly mobilized its frontline presence, coordinating with host governments, UN sister agencies, and local partners under the inter-agency Yemen Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan (HNRP). UNHCR’s response in Yemen has prioritized protection, emergency cash assistance, emergency shelter, core relief items, and water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) interventions. In Djibouti, UNHCR is supporting the Governmentled response, leading the coordination of UN agencies and local partners under the Refugee Coordination Model, and continues to invest in a cohesive response to the emergency, ensuring Government-led efforts towards registration and refugee village expansions are sustainable and avoid parallel structures. In Somalia, while movements remained relatively limited, UNHCR has worked closely with local authorities in Somaliland and in Puntland, as well as humanitarian partners to strengthen reception, protection and emergency preparedness in anticipation of potential further arrivals.

items.title: Humanitarian Needs and Response Trends in Northeast Nigeria, 2022-2026: A Five-Year Retrospective Analysis (November 2026)
items.blurb:
Country: Nigeria
Source: Voices and Evidence Frontiers

Please refer to the attached file.

Executive Summary

Over time, coordinated humanitarian response in Northeast Nigeria has progressed with minimal multi-year evidence and insight captured across annual datasets. This retrospective longitudinal analysis of secondary humanitarian datasets synthesizes five years of UNOCHA needs and planning datasets from 2022 to 2026 to extract actionable lessons for the future.

An examination of needs and demographic trends reveals that the crisis remains protracted, with deep vulnerabilities persisting across total People in Need (PiN). Over the five-year period, Borno consistently remained the epicenter of the crisis, while Yobe’s caseload held steady despite tighter counting boundaries in 2026. Demographically, females consistently accounted for the majority of people in need every year, while Host Communities remained the largest share of the affected population amid declining internally displaced person (IDP) and returnee proportions. Financial and operational data further demonstrates how shrinking resource envelopes reshaped the delivery architecture. A deliberate narrowing of targeting coverage became necessary as funding shrank. Simultaneously, National NGOs (NNGOs) steadily expanded their operational share to become the primary delivery backbone as International NGOs (INGOs) drew down.
Drawing on insights from the data, organizations must transition toward multi-year, cross-cutting resilience programming and diversify funding beyond traditional Humanitarian appeals. Donors and cluster leads should enforce dedicated gender-responsive funding quotas while investing in institutional capacity and direct financing for national partners. Additionally, humanitarian actors should tailor interventions to the distinct operational realities of Borno, Adamawa, and Yobe states rather than applying a uniform regional template.

items.title: Yemen: Catastrophic civilian suffering as donors and media look elsewhere | NRC
items.blurb:
Country: Yemen
Source: Norwegian Refugee Council

Intensifying conflict is driving horrific levels of harm and deepening humanitarian needs across Yemen, warned Jan Egeland, Secretary General of the Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC), during a visit to the country this week.

Press release

Yemen Published 26. Nov 2026

Yemen entered this year as one of the most profound and most neglected humanitarian crises. Renewed fighting and airstrikes along multiple frontlines have uprooted hundreds of thousands of people. Despite shocking levels of suffering, the international response has withered, and conflict and civilian harm continues unabated.

In the north, home to most of the country’s population, a handful of overstretched and underfunded national and international organisations are the only remaining lifeline to millions in need. Severe funding reductions, sanctions, and the UN’s ongoing pause in its operations following detention of their aid workers have all contributed to a collapsing humanitarian response, compounded by the insecurity and access constraints.

“The situation across the country was already catastrophic, with long-term displacement and long-term humanitarian needs growing almost entirely out of sight,” said Egeland. “But now fighting has again displaced entire communities, while disrupted supply routes have driven up food and fuel prices. Across the country, families who were already struggling to survive are being pushed deeper into hunger."

Yemen’s humanitarian response faces a severe lack of funding, which can be measured by the hundreds of thousands of families who will receive no support despite being in desperate need. Just 12 per cent of funding for emergency shelter support has been received so far, drastically reducing the ability of organisations to provide any shelter support to displaced people.

“Everywhere I have been, there are people searching for food or water, children are out of school, and parents desperately worrying about how to keep their children safe. I’ve met newly displaced people forced to shelter under the leaves of banana trees propped up with sticks,” said Egeland. “I’ve seen many families receiving no aid at all, while our courageous humanitarian colleagues struggle to increase emergency relief as well as minimal services for people who have remain displaced for years.

“All parties to the conflict bear responsibility for the vast scale of harm here. All must commit, in full, to protecting civilians and facilitating a humanitarian response at the scale that Yemenis need. The powerful countries backing the armed actors must commit to making this a reality.

“Across Yemen, I’ve been meeting with NRC teams and other humanitarians who are simply desperate to do more, but conflict and access restrictions, and the lack of funding, are preventing us from meeting even the most urgent needs. The suffering caused by cruel violence in Yemen is compounded by diplomatic and funding negligence of the highest order,” said Egeland.

Notes to editors:

  • Photos from Egeland’s visit are available for free use here.
  • 321,000 people have been displaced in Yemen since the escalation broke out in August (OCHA).
  • Yemen’s 2026 humanitarian response is 23 per cent funded at 500.8 million US dollars out of 2.16 billion required (OCHA).
  • In 2023 Yemen received 1.77 billion US dollars, approximately 41% of the 4.3 billion US dollars required to assist 17.3 million people. By November 2026, only 500 million US dollars had been secured – 23% of the 2.16 billion US dollars required. This is a 72 per cent decline in funding against increasing needs (OCHA).
  • 23.1 million people across Yemen are in need of lifesaving humanitarian assistance, representing more than 65 per cent of the entire population (OCHA).
  • 18.3 million people in Yemen face food insecurity (WFP).
  • Since the escalation in August, 4,998 families have newly arrived at NRC-supported sites including 1,350 new families in Taiz, 3,130 new households in Abyan, and 518 new families in Lahj.
  • The 2026 Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan aimed, before the escalation, to reach a much-reduced target of 12 million people, even while 22 million people require assistance(HNRP). Just 16 per cent of the funding required to support food security has been received, 22 per cent for WASH, and just 12 per cent for shelter, substantially limiting assistance to vulnerable communities (OCHA).
  • Yemen featured 4th on NRC’s annual list of the world’s most neglected displacement crises this year (NRC).
  • NRC supports 25 displacement sites for internally displaced persons (IDPs) in governorates hosting people fleeing the current fighting in Taiz governorate and the West Coast.

items.title: From Rainfall Forecasts to Anticipatory Action: A Flood Digital Twin at Work in Dolo Ado, Ethiopia (November 2026)
items.blurb:
Country: Ethiopia
Source: CGIAR

Please refer to the attached file.

Citation

Haile, Alemseged Tamiru, Eden Seifu Gebre, Getahun Kebede Mengistie, Abel Negussie Alemu, and Hugox Retief. 2026. From Rainfall Forecasts to Anticipatory Action: A Flood Digital Twin at Work in Dolo Ado, Ethiopia. International Water Management Institute.

Abstract/Description

Flood Early Warning Bulletins translate forecasts into clear, timely, actionable information for preparedness, anticipatory action, and emergency response. By presenting expected conditions, potential impacts, and recommended actions in a standard format, they help government agencies, humanitarian organizations, and at-risk communities coordinate decisions before floods occur. Yet fragmented datasets, disconnected modelling workflows, and manual processes often delay bulletins and shorten the time available to protect lives, livelihoods, and infrastructure.

To address this gap, the International Water Management Institute (IWMI), national government institutions, and development partners developed the Dolo Ado Digital Twin-based Flood Early Warning System. It creates a digital replica of the floodplain, enables two-way data exchange with communities, and integrates global databases, field surveys, and district data. HEC-HMS converts rainfall forecasts into flood forecasts, while HEC-RAS simulates likely inundation, including water depth and flood duration across the river and floodplain.

A key achievement is the co-created Flood Early Warning Bulletin, refined by stakeholders through consultations, co-design workshops, technical training, and continuous feedback. An automated workflow rapidly converts reliable Digital Twin forecasts into standardized warnings, with content, visuals, terminology, and format tailored to operational needs. The bulletin enables government agencies, humanitarian organizations, and disaster risk management authorities to make timely, coordinated decisions before and during floods.

items.title: World: ¿Cómo acompañar a sobrevivientes de violencia basada en género?
items.blurb:
Country: World
Source: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies

En contextos de conflicto y crisis, hasta el 70 % de las mujeres enfrenta algún tipo de violencia. Reconocer esta realidad, diseñar soluciones para protegerlas y apostar por formas de trabajo que no perpetúen las amenazas contra la vida y el bienestar de las mujeres es una de nuestras prioridades. En este artículo compartimos recomendaciones para ofrecer una respuesta humanitaria segura, digna y sin revictimización.

Cuando ocurre una emergencia o un desastre, las redes de apoyo institucional y comunitario se debilitan, los medios de vida se interrumpen y las desigualdades y vulnerabilidades previas se agudizan. Como resultado, en entornos afectados por crisis, hasta el 70 % de las mujeres enfrenta situaciones de violencia, casi el doble de la tasa registrada fuera de las zonas de crisis.

El desafío es aún más urgente ante las brechas globales de prevención y atención a la violencia. Solo en 2025, se reportó que el 50% de las personas sobrevivientes de violencia basada en género (VBG) no tuvo acceso a servicios esenciales como espacios seguros, atención médica, apoyo psicosocial, protección o asistencia legal, dejando al menos a un millón de mujeres y niñas sin atención vital.

Al mismo tiempo, las organizaciones de mujeres reportan un aumento en la demanda de servicios desde enero de 2025 e indican que la mayoría ya no logran cubrir los niveles actuales de necesidad en un momento marcado por recortes al financiamiento humanitario.

En los 16 Días de Activismo contra la Violencia de Género, que se extienden del 25 de noviembre, Día Internacional de la Eliminación de la Violencia contra la Mujer, al 10 de diciembre, Día de los Derechos Humanos, la Federación Internacional de Sociedades de la Cruz Roja y de la Media Luna Roja (IFRC) reafirma la prioridad de poner en el centro la protección de las sobrevivientes en cada respuesta de emergencia.

Los equipos humanitarios deben actuar bajo la premisa de que la violencia basada en género ocurre en toda crisis y deben tomar medidas de protección coherentes con las normas humanitarias, existan o no denuncias o pruebas concretas.

Reconocer todas las caras de la violencia y actuar desde lo local

Una vida libre de violencia, la igualdad de género y el reparto equitativo de las responsabilidades familiares entre hombres y mujeres son esenciales para el bienestar personal y social. Para prevenir y responder de forma efectiva, el primer paso práctico es reconocer que la violencia basada en género adopta múltiples formas, muchas veces invisibilizadas:

  • Violencia sexual y abuso sexual.
  • Violencia doméstica o intrafamiliar.
  • Violencia económica (control o privación de recursos financieros).
  • Matrimonio forzado o precoz.
  • Prostitución forzada y explotación sexual.

Dentro de los espacios de voluntariado de la Cruz Roja y la Media Luna Roja en todo el mundo, el liderazgo y la experiencia de las mujeres son indispensables para construir sistemas de protección seguros y eficaces.

La prevención comienza desde el diseño mismo de las operaciones, desde habilitar espacios seguros para mujeres, niñez y poblaciones LGBTQIA+, hasta garantizar insumos dignos para la gestión de la salud menstrual, mapear rutas de derivación segura e impulsar la representación diversa en todos los niveles de liderazgo.

5 claves para acompañar con dignidad y no hacer daño

Todas las acciones para abordar la violencia basada en género deben regirse por el principio de no hacer daño y estar centradas en la persona sobreviviente. Si una persona comparte una situación de violencia, estas cinco pautas guían una primera respuesta ética y segura:

1. Escuchar sin juzgar ni interrumpir

Para asegurar la comodidad y seguridad de la persona, es importante habilitar un espacio privado, confidencial y seguro. Escuche con atención como parte de los primeros auxilios psicológicos, sin emitir opiniones, cuestionamientos ni juicios sobre lo ocurrido. Permita que la persona exprese sus emociones libremente, sin minimizar sus sentimientos ni darle consejos no solicitados.

2. Pedir consentimiento y respetar la confidencialidad

El personal humanitario debe respetar los tiempos de la persona sobreviviente y evitar presionarla para que cuente más de lo que desea. Pedirle que repita su relato una y otra vez, o hacer interrogatorios detallados sin ser personal especializado genera revictimización. La labor humanitaria no es investigar, sino acompañar y facilitar derivaciones seguras. Además, nunca se deben compartir los datos ni derivar un caso adulto sin su consentimiento expreso e informado, salvo que exista un riesgo vital inminente.

3. Adaptar el entorno y asegurar la inclusión

Cuando acompañamos a una persona que ha sobrevivido a violencia de género debemos garantizar un trato afirmativo, accesible y libre de prejuicios, asegurando que ninguna persona esté desprotegida.

Las mujeres y niñas con discapacidad enfrentan tasas más altas de violencia y suelen contar con menos servicios adaptados. Podemos eliminar barreras físicas y comunicacionales utilizando lenguaje claro, apoyo visual o intérpretes si es necesario, e involucrpandoles activamente en el diseño de las soluciones.

También debemos evitar suposiciones sobre el género u orientación sexual de la persona, y utilizar siempre el nombre y los pronombres que la persona indique.

Asegurar la inclusión implica facilitar que la persona se involucre activamente en cada decisión sobre su proceso, ejerciendo sus derechos, deseos y la seguridad de su familia.

4. Realizar derivaciones seguras de emergencias médicas

La violencia sexual es una emergencia médica que requiere atención en las primeras 72 horas para prevenir infecciones de transmisión sexual (incluido el VIH), embarazos no deseados y secuelas físicas o psicológicas. Compartir información confiable y accesible sobre los servicios médicos, psicosociales, legales y de apoyo económico disponibles en la comunidad, es parte de la atención en salud. Esta acción no condiciona al personal de salud a presentar una denuncia, pero sí conecta a la persona con redes especializadas de forma segura y confidencial.

5. Proteger a la niñez y adolescencia

La protección de la niñez y la adolescencia es una responsabilidad compartida y exige protocolos estrictos para no exponer a la niñez y la adolescencia a mayores riesgos.

En un entorno privado y seguro, debemos asegurarnos de que la persona menor de edad sepa que vamos a creer en su palabra y que sabemos que no fue su culpa.

Si existe peligro inminente, debemos resguardar al niño, niña o adolescente lejos de la persona agresora, sin confrontarla directamente para evitar riesgos mayores y activa de inmediato las alertas ante las autoridades de protección y seguridad correspondientes.

Posteriormente debemos derivar el caso hacia los organismos oficiales de protección de la infancia y servicios especializados de salud y primeros auxilios psicológicos, evitando entrevistas profundas que puedan causar revictimización.

El personal humanitario también debe mantener acompañada e informada a la familia o red segura durante todo el proceso.

Prevención y cuidados desde el terreno

Proteger a las comunidades exige que las operaciones humanitarias sean un entorno íntegro y seguro. En la IFRC rige una política estricta de Tolerancia Cero frente a cualquier forma de acoso, discriminación, explotación o abuso sexual.

Las reglas de salvaguarda son innegociables para todo el personal y el voluntariado:

  • Cero tolerancia a cualquier actividad sexual con niños, niñas y adolescentes.
  • Está estrictamente prohibido ofrecer dinero, empleo, bienes, servicios o asistencia humanitaria a cambio de favores sexuales.
  • No se permiten relaciones sexuales entre el personal humanitario y las personas atendidas, ni el uso indebido del cargo o la jerarquía.

Cualquier sospecha de conducta indebida, explotación, abuso sexual, acoso o vulneración de la integridad puede reportarse de forma segura y confidencial a través de la línea de integridad de la IFRC en www.ifrc.integrityline.org, al correo electrónico [email protected] o llamando de manera gratuita al +41 800 437 272.

Un llamado urgente a la acción

La violencia contra las mujeres y las niñas es una violación de los derechos humanos para la que no existe excusa. Para revertir esta crisis, la red de la IFRC hace un llamado a gobiernos, donantes y organizaciones aliadas a actuar en cinco frentes prioritarios:

  • Proteger a las personas sobrevivientes.
  • Mantener los servicios esenciales y salvaguardar su financiamiento sostenido.
  • Garantizar la justicia y la rendición de cuentas para poner fin a la impunidad.
  • Fortalecer la prevención y respuesta lideradas localmente, invirtiendo en el liderazgo de las mujeres.
  • Integrar la protección en cada etapa de la acción humanitaria.

Los derechos humanos pertenecen a todas las personas; la seguridad también debe serlo. Erradicar la violencia contra las mujeres y las niñas es una tarea colectiva que empieza por creer, escuchar sin prejuicios y garantizar que cada espacio de apoyo sea verdaderamente seguro y digno.

items.title: World: How can we support survivors of gender-based violence?
items.blurb:
Country: World
Source: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies

In conflict and crisis settings, up to 70% of women face some form of violence. Recognizing this reality, designing solutions to protect them, and committing to ways of working that do not perpetuate threats to women's lives and well-being is one of our priorities. In this article, we share recommendations for delivering a safe, dignified humanitarian response that avoids revictimization.

When an emergency or disaster strikes, institutional and community support networks weaken, livelihoods are disrupted, and pre-existing inequalities and vulnerabilities deepen. As a result, in crisis-affected settings, up to 70% of women experience violence, nearly double the rate recorded outside crisis zones.

The challenge is even more urgent given global gaps in violence prevention and care. In 2025 alone, 50% of survivors of gender-based violence (GBV) were reported to lack access to essential services such as safe spaces, health care, psychosocial support, protection, or legal assistance, leaving at least one million women and girls without vital care.

At the same time, women's organizations report an increase in demand for services since January 2025 and indicate that most can no longer meet current levels of need at a time marked by humanitarian funding cuts.

During the 16 Days of Activism Against Gender-Based Violence, running from November 25, the International Day for the Elimination of Violence Against Women, to December 10, International Human Rights Day, the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) reaffirms its priority of placing the protection of survivors at the centre of every emergency response.

Humanitarian teams must operate on the premise that gender-based violence occurs in every crisis and must take protective measures consistent with humanitarian standards, whether or not formal reports or concrete evidence exist.

Recognizing all forms of violence and acting locally

A life free from violence, gender equality, and the equitable sharing of family responsibilities between women and men are essential for personal and social well-being. To prevent and respond effectively, the first practical step is recognizing that gender-based violence takes many forms, often hidden from view:

  • Sexual violence and sexual abuse.
  • Domestic or intimate partner violence.
  • Economic violence (control or deprivation of financial resources).
  • Forced or child marriage.
  • Forced prostitution and sexual exploitation.

Within Red Cross and Red Crescent volunteering spaces worldwide, women's leadership and expertise are indispensable to building safe and effective protection systems.

Prevention begins at the very design stage of operations, from setting up safe spaces for women, children, and LGBTQIA+ populations, to ensuring dignified supplies for menstrual health management, mapping safe referral pathways, and promoting diverse representation at all levels of leadership.

5 keys to supporting survivors with dignity and doing no harm

All actions to address gender-based violence must be guided by the "do no harm" principle and remain survivor-centred. If someone discloses an experience of violence, these five guidelines steer an ethical and safe initial response:

1. Listen without judging or interrupting

To ensure the person's comfort and safety, provide a private, confidential, and safe space. Listen attentively as part of psychological first aid, without offering opinions, questioning, or judging what happened. Allow the person to express their emotions freely, without minimizing their feelings or giving unsolicited advice.

2. Ask for consent and respect confidentiality

Humanitarian personnel must respect the survivor's pace and avoid pressuring them to share more than they wish. Asking them to repeat their story over and over, or conducting detailed questioning without specialized training, causes revictimization. Humanitarian work is not about investigating, but about supporting and facilitating safe referrals. Furthermore, personal data must never be shared, nor an adult case referred, without the survivor's express and informed consent, unless there is an imminent threat to life.

3. Adapt the environment and ensure inclusion

When supporting a survivor of gender-based violence, we must guarantee affirmative, accessible, and bias-free treatment, ensuring that no one is left unprotected.

Women and girls with disabilities experience higher rates of violence and often have fewer accessible services available to them. We can remove physical and communication barriers by using clear language, visual aids, or interpreters when needed, and by actively involving them in designing solutions.

We must also avoid making assumptions about a person's gender or sexual orientation, and always use the name and pronouns they indicate.

Ensuring inclusion means enabling the person to participate actively in every decision regarding their process, upholding their rights, wishes, and the safety of their family.

4. Make safe referrals for medical emergencies

Sexual violence is a medical emergency that requires care within the first 72 hours to prevent sexually transmitted infections (including HIV), unintended pregnancies, and physical or psychological harm. Sharing reliable, accessible information about medical, psychosocial, legal, and economic support services available in the community is part of health care. This action does not obligate health personnel to file a legal report, but it connects the person with specialized networks safely and confidentially.

5. Protect children and adolescents

Protecting children and adolescents is a shared responsibility and requires strict protocols to avoid exposing them to further harm.

In a private and safe environment, we must ensure the child or adolescent knows we believe them and that what happened was not their fault.

If there is imminent danger, we must move the child or adolescent away from the perpetrator, without confronting the perpetrator directly to avoid greater risks, and immediately alert the relevant child protection and safety authorities.

Subsequently, we must refer the case to official child protection agencies and specialized health and psychological first aid services, avoiding in-depth interviews that could cause revictimization.

Humanitarian personnel must also keep the family or safe support network accompanied and informed throughout the entire process.

Prevention and care from the field

Protecting communities requires humanitarian operations to be safe environments of high integrity. The IFRC enforces a strict Zero Tolerance policy against any form of harassment, discrimination, sexual exploitation, or abuse.

Safeguarding rules are non-negotiable for all staff and volunteers:

  • Zero tolerance for any sexual activity with children and adolescents.
  • Offering money, employment, goods, services, or humanitarian assistance in exchange for sexual favours is strictly prohibited.
  • Sexual relationships between humanitarian personnel and the people they assist, as well as any misuse of position or hierarchy, are prohibited.

Any suspicion of misconduct, sexual exploitation and abuse, harassment, or integrity violations can be reported safely and confidentially through the IFRC Integrity Line at www.ifrc.integrityline.org, by email at [email protected], or by calling toll-free at +41 800 437 272.

An urgent call to action

Violence against women and girls is a human rights violation for which there is no excuse. To reverse this crisis, the IFRC network calls on governments, donors, and partner organizations to act on five priority fronts:

  • Maintain essential services and safeguard sustained funding.
  • Ensure justice and accountability to end impunity.
  • Strengthen locally led prevention and response by investing in women's leadership.
  • Integrate protection into every stage of humanitarian action.

Human rights belong to everyone; safety must too. Ending violence against women and girls is a collective effort that begins with believing, listening without prejudice, and ensuring that every space of support is truly safe and dignified.

items.title: Pronunciamiento del Equipo Humanitario País sobre la protección de la población civil en Colombia - 25/11/2026
items.blurb:
Country: Colombia
Sources: El Equipo Humanitario País Colombia, UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs

Please refer to the attached file.

Bogotá, 25 de noviembre 2026

Las agencias de Naciones Unidas y las organizaciones humanitarias que integran el Equipo Humanitario de País (EHP) de Colombia notan con preocupación el deterioro de las condiciones de seguridad y sus consecuencias humanitarias, así como por la persistencia y expansión de graves riesgos para la población civil en distintas subregiones del país como el pacífico, nororiente, noroccidente y suroccidente del país.

El Equipo Humanitario País hace un llamado urgente a todos los actores armados para adoptar y fortalecer todas las medidas necesarias para prevenir daños y proteger a la población civil, respetando plenamente las normas del Derecho Internacional Humanitario (DIH), incluidos los principios de distinción, proporcionalidad y precaución. La población civil, los bienes de carácter civil y la infraestructura indispensable para su supervivencia deben ser protegidos en todo momento y permanecer al margen de las hostilidades.

Asimismo, el Equipo Humanitario País recuerda que la acción humanitaria se guía por los principios de humanidad, neutralidad, imparcialidad e independencia, que permiten brindar asistencia exclusivamente en función de las necesidades de las personas afectadas, sin discriminación. El respeto de estos principios por todas las partes es esencial para prevenir mayores afectaciones, preservar el espacio humanitario y generar las condiciones necesarias para llegar a las comunidades vulnerables que requieren asistencia y protección con el objetivo de salvar vidas. En este contexto, el Equipo Humanitario País hace un llamado a prevenir y eliminar las restricciones que puedan poner en riesgo a las comunidades o impedir la acción humanitaria, y a garantizar un acceso humanitario seguro,
oportuno, sostenido y sin obstáculos.

El Equipo Humanitario País reafirma su compromiso de continuar acompañando de manera coordinada a las comunidades afectadas y fortaleciendo las acciones de prevención y respuesta humanitaria, sobre la base de los principios humanitarios y del respeto del Derecho Internacional Humanitario, como se ha realizado en las últimas décadas.

Asimismo, reiteran su disposición a contribuir a generar las condiciones necesarias para prevenir nuevas afectaciones, promover la protección de la población civil y asegurar que la asistencia humanitaria llegue de manera segura a quienes más la necesitan.

items.title: Cameroon Cholera Outbreak: Situation Report #8 (November 25, 2026)
items.blurb:
Country: Cameroon
Source: International Medical Corps

Please refer to the attached file.

FAST FACTS

  • 462 suspected cholera cases and four deaths (0.87% CFR) were recorded in Minawao Refugee Camp between July 24 and October 17, with zero new cases for 29 consecutive days as of November 15.
  • Minawao hosts more than 81,000 refugees—more than triple its intended capacity (325%)—resulting in an attack rate of 570 cases per 100,000 inhabitants.
  • Across Cameroon’s Far North Region, 3,038 cases (15% in Minawao) and 86 deaths (2.83% case-fatality rate) were recorded across 18 health districts as of November 9, with the last regional case reported on October 28.
  • Though active cholera transmission inside Minawao has stopped, the wider regional outbreak has not yet been declared over. Overcrowding, cross-border mobility and unresolved water and sanitation gaps sustain the risk of reintroduction into the camp.

OUR RESPONSE

  • Operating in Minawao Refugee Camp since 2013, International Medical Corps launched an emergency cholera response within 24 hours of the initial alert on July 24, supporting the Mokolo Health District with pre-positioned contingency stocks.
  • We expanded the camp’s existing 15-bed treatment unit to 100 beds using temporary overflow tents and 37 clinical and support staff.
  • We trained, equipped and supervised 90 refugee community health workers (CHWs) across all camp blocks, who conducted 140,000+ household visits, traced 3,400+ contacts, and disinfected 8,000+ households and community spaces.
  • Deployed all 90 CHWs as volunteer vaccinators—helping to reach 75,444 people (92.6% coverage)—and documented operational lessons to strengthen readiness for future outbreaks.

items.title: World: Protecting Children from Air Pollution: Applying the social and behaviour change message guidance in the REACH Framework
items.blurb:
Country: World
Source: UN Children's Fund

Please refer to the attached file.

Highlights

Air pollution is the single biggest environmental threat to child health. Around 930 million children, 4 in 10 worldwide, breathe outdoor air with a level of fine particles seven times that considered safe by the World Health Organization. Every day, almost 2,000 children under 5 years of age die from air-pollution-related causes, accounting for more than one in four of all deaths in this age group. Three quarters of these deaths are linked to air pollution inside the home.

Yet it's one of the hardest risks to communicate, because the harm is invisible, cumulative, and easily normalized. This new guide offers a framework for messages that move families and decision makers from awareness to sustained protective action, organized around the REACH (recognize, engage, act, context, habit) framework and designed to be localized to each setting.

items.title: World: UN Women statement for International Women Human Rights Defenders Day 2026
items.blurb:
Country: World
Source: UN Women

UN Women stands in solidarity with all women human rights defenders and all those who defend the rights of women and girls.

On International Women Human Rights Defenders Day (29 November), we recognize an incontestable fact: Women human rights defenders and feminist movements drive progress on women’s rights. They organize, pursue justice, challenge discrimination, and create space for others to participate. Yet their ability to do this work continues to face increasing pressure.

Seven in 10 women human rights defenders, activists, and journalists surveyed by UN Women experienced online violence in the course of their work. Four in 10 reported related harm offline.

For some, defending human rights comes at the cost of their freedom or their lives. According to OHCHR, 813 women human rights defenders, journalists, and trade unionists were killed or subjected to enforced disappearance between 2015 and 2025.

Despite these threats, women human rights defenders and feminist movements continue to push forward: to mobilize, build coalitions, demand accountability, and defend hard-won gains. Their work is more critical than ever.

We know what needs to be done. UN Women calls on governments and all relevant actors to protect women human rights defenders, both online and offline; hold perpetrators of violence and intimidation accountable; guarantee defenders’ meaningful participation in decision-making; and provide sustained and flexible funding for their work.

On this International Women Human Rights Defenders Day, UN Women stands in solidarity with all women human rights defenders and all those who defend the rights of women and girls.

An attack on those who defend women’s rights is an attack on progress for us all. Protecting them is protecting our collective future.

1. About LTC Logs - Common Services SOP

This document provides an overview of the common logistics services made available through the Logistics & Telecommunications Cluster (LTC), how to access them and the conditions under which these services are to be provided. The objective of these services is to support humanitarian organisations in sustaining relief and early recovery operations through coordinated logistics services and operational information to the affected population in Nepal.

These services are not intended to replace the logistics capacities of other organisations, nor are they meant to compete with the commercial market. Rather, they are intended to fill identified operational gaps and provide a last-resort option in case other service providers are not available, and/or existing capacity is inadequate to respond to humanitarian needs.

These services are planned to be available until 31 December 2026, with the possibility of further extension. However, partial or complete withdrawal of the services may occur prior to this date due to specific circumstances:

  • Services are no longer an agreed upon/identified need
  • Funding constraints

This document is subject to regular updates based on evolving operational requirements and situational changes. Service requestors are responsible for consulting the latest version prior to submitting any requests. Updated versions will be shared on the Nepal Operations page.

items.title: ‘The Kids Love It’: Meet the B’luru Mum Turning 100 Kg of Waste Fabric Into Decor You Can Rent
items.blurb: What’s a birthday party without balloons? For Bengaluru-based entrepreneur and mother of two, Sowmya Jagannath, this was a question she found herself thinking about while planning her daughter’s birthday. She wanted to try something different, but would her daughter feel that something was missing? Her daughter loves animals, so Sowmya chose colourful fabric decorations in green and earthy shades. Fabric bunting hung across the room, bringing the animal-themed party to life. There were no balloons to inflate or plastic streamers to pull down after the guests left. Instead, the decorations could be packed away and used again at another celebration. The children had fun, and all of Sowmya’s initial worries turned out to be unnecessary. Neither her daughter nor the other children missed the balloons. The decorations came from Matter Party, a Bengaluru-based startup that rents out reusable party décor made from post-consumer textile waste. Founded by Bhavna Kanoria in March 2025, it offers themed fabric decorations that families can rent, return and pass on for another celebration, instead of buying new items that may be discarded after a single use. For Bhavna, the idea began at home, when her own daughter asked for a planet-themed birthday party. The two made buntings from an old sari , finding a way to make the occasion special with fabric they already had. What began with making planet-themed bunting from an old sari for her daughter's birthday eventually inspired Bhavna to start Matter Party in Bengaluru. That small experiment stayed with Bhavna. It would eventually become a business built around a simple question: could celebrations be beautiful, convenient and less wasteful at the same time? How an old sari sparked a business idea Bhavna has a master’s degree in English literature, studied interior design and previously worked as a designer. She had also explored ways of making gifting more thoughtful through earlier ventures, including a gift registry service called Giftistree and Scift, a social gifting platform that allowed people to donate to a cause instead of giving physical presents. The idea for Matter Party, however, took time to develop. After making the fabric bunting with her daughter, Bhavna left it on the back burner for a few years. Towards the end of 2024, she returned to it, thinking about how the same principle could work on a larger scale. Matter Party launched in March 2025. Her first rental was for a Lohri celebration rather than a birthday party. The booking came through a friend of a friend, giving her an early opportunity to see how the idea might work beyond her own home. The business now sources post-consumer textile waste through Hasiru Dala, a Bengaluru-based waste management organisation with a textile recovery facility. Bhavna buys discarded fabric by weight, with material sorted by colour, and sends it to a tailoring unit to be stitched into decorations. “I work on the designs and handle much of the finishing myself, including attaching cords by hand. The leftover scraps are returned to the recovery facility,” she says. The result is a collection of reusable decorations in around 35 themes, from unicorns and dinosaurs to Superman, Harry Potter, rainbows and rustic-chic themes. Families can mix and match colours to suit their party. Matter Party sources post-consumer textile waste through Hasiru Dala and transforms the discarded fabric into colourful party decorations. Lightweight and fitted with cords at both ends, the pieces can be tied to existing fixtures without complicated installation. Once a party is over, the kit is collected and prepared for its next outing. Bhavna irons the fabric, spot-cleans it with soap and water, replaces cords where needed and checks the decorations before they are rented out again. The aim is to keep the materials in use for as long as possible. For these decorations to make their way into more homes, Bhavna knew she had to make renting them as easy as possible for busy parents. What makes parents choose reusable decorations? When Bhavna began offering reusable party décor, she realised that leading with sustainability did not always persuade people to try it. “People may not choose it just because it is sustainable,” she explains. For many parents, the first questions are more practical: Will the decorations look good? Will they suit the theme? Will they be easy to put up? Will renting them be worth the cost? Each decoration is designed to be used across multiple celebrations, allowing families to rent, return and reuse party décor instead of buying new ones. That understanding has influenced how she presents Matter Party. She wants families to choose the decorations for their designs, range of choices and convenience, without feeling that they have to compromise on how their child's birthday party looks. The reduced pricing is another part of making the service accessible. The startup currently offers two rental options: a Mini Kit for Rs 1,750, which includes 8-10 buntings and fringes, suited to home parties and smaller venues, and a Party Kit for Rs 3,500, with 16-20 buntings and fringes for larger spaces such as clubhouses and gardens. Both kits also include door or backdrop nets, wreaths and a ‘Happy Birthday’ banner. A refundable security deposit is charged separately. Customers can book through WhatsApp, choose a kit and arrange for delivery before their event. The decorations are collected after the celebration, so families do not have to find storage space for items they may use only once a year. Bhavna has also tried to make the process of putting up and taking down the decorations simple. The kits arrive ready to use, with cords that can be tied to existing fixtures, and customers can pack them back into the provided bag after the party. Optional party helpers are also available through a service partner for families who need additional support. Sowmya found that the rental model made financial sense, too. When she compared the cost with what she had spent buying decorations separately, she realised how quickly individual purchases could add up. “I had done a calculation of the cost of the balloons and the buntings and all the other stuff that I had bought the previous year, and this was actually cheaper than that. We don't realise because we buy it in parts. One balloon package, one streamer package, then this and that. By the time you add it all up, it actually comes up to the same thing, if not more,” she says. From dinosaurs and unicorns to rainbows and Harry Potter, Bhavna's reusable fabric decorations are available in around 35 themes for families to choose from. For Bhavna, this is the kind of shift that could help reusable décor reach more families: it needs to meet their everyday needs as well as help them reduce waste. 'The children don't miss the balloons' Sowmya has used Matter Party for celebrations built around her children’s changing interests. Along with her daughter’s animal-themed party, her son has had a Harry Potter-inspired celebration in red and black, and the family has also tried a cricket theme. “The themes will be there, but colours are always the easiest thing to put together in terms of adding that vibe to the party. I love that she has so many different colour options,” she says. The designs have also drawn attention from other parents. At her daughter’s birthday in September, guests could not stop admiring the décor. Those conversations have given Sowmya a chance to talk about the idea with other families. An earlier conversation with Bhavna about balloons and the impact they can have on animals had encouraged Sowmya to try celebrating without them. “I was almost scared because I was like, ‘Oh my God, if I don't have balloons at the party, how will I manage? Will my daughter be okay?’” she recalls. But the children were happy without them. “Nobody missed the balloon completely. Sometimes you have to take these steps to experience yourself; a balloon is not everything for a party,” she says. Shwetha, another Bengaluru-based mother of two girls aged 13 and nine, came to Matter Party for a similar mix of thoughtful design and a more sustainable approach. After every celebration, Bhavna irons and spot-cleans the fabric decorations, replaces cords where needed and prepares the kits for their next rental. “I would try and reuse as much as possible, but having said that, options were limited. So I was very pleased that Bhavna came out with a solution which was a little more comprehensive,” she says. Shweta has since used the kits for her daughters’ birthdays, including garden and rainbow themes. She likes the range of choices and the convenience of having the décor delivered and collected. A small placard explaining that the decorations are sustainable also gives guests a way to understand the idea. “Keeping sustainability aside, the design is impeccable. She's thought of various options that you would want to host a party. It's definitely something that people should go for even keeping sustainability outside of it,” Shweta says. For Bhavna, feedback like this reinforces the importance of making reusable décor attractive and practical in its own right. Over 100 kg of fabric gets a second life Since its launch, Matter Party has upcycled more than 100 kg of post-consumer textile waste and catered to 64 parties and events. For now, the startup operates only in Bengaluru. Bhavna is mindful of the emissions involved in transporting the kits over long distances and does not want expansion to undermine the purpose of the business. She is also exploring collaborations with party venues, cafés, restaurants and other vendors, along with workshops in schools that could help children understand how celebrations can generate less waste. The business has grown through repeat customers and word of mouth, but Bhavna knows that making sustainable choices commonplace will take more than one rental service. It also means helping families see that they do not have to give up the excitement or personal touches that make a birthday special. That change can extend beyond the decorations. Sowmya, for instance, has given plants as return gifts at her daughter’s birthday and has chosen plantable pencils and stationery on another occasion. Bengaluru mother Sowmya Jagannath chose Matter Party's reusable fabric decorations for her daughter's animal-themed birthday, celebrating without balloons. Shweta says using the kits has made her think about what else she might change when planning an event. Bhavna has noticed a similar openness among children in her own family. Her niece and nephew, aged three and six, have started telling their friends to avoid waste. For her, it is a reminder that children can adapt to different ways of celebrating, particularly when those choices are part of the experience from the beginning. Helping families celebrate with less waste Bhavna hopes to grow Matter Party without losing sight of what made her start it: the possibility of making a familiar part of family life less wasteful, without making it less joyful. She does not expect parents to change every habit at once. Choosing reusable decorations, skipping balloons or rethinking return gifts can be a starting point. “The aim is to make these options feel normal rather than like an extra effort reserved for particularly environmentally conscious families,” she adds. Since launching in March 2025, Matter Party has upcycled over 100 kg of textile waste and catered to 64 parties and events. That is also why she wants to expand through local partnerships instead of simply shipping kits across the country. For her, the way the business operates matters as much as the product it offers. A birthday party may last only a few hours, but the decorations can be part of many more celebrations. For Bhavna, that is the possibility she wants more parents to discover: the colourful bunting that made one child's birthday special could bring just as much joy to another child, without either family having to buy everything new. items.title: 5 Artists Used Bamboo, Thread & Even Egg Trays To Create India’s Award-Winning Venice Exhibition
items.blurb: When the Delhi house where artist Sumakshi Singh spent her childhood summers was demolished, she found an extraordinary way to bring it back. Using delicate white threads, she recreated its doors, windows, stairs and even its gates. Thousands of kilometres away in Venice, Italy, her childhood home became part of an exhibition that drew around 4.5 lakh visitors. Alongside her work stood a towering bamboo structure inspired by Indian construction sites, a miniature Ladakhi settlement made from discarded egg trays and paper, and sculptures inspired by India’s natural landscapes. On 25 November 2026, these creations earned India the Visitors’ Lion for Best National Participation at the Venice Biennale, one of the world’s biggest international art exhibitions. The award was decided by public vote. The winning exhibition brought together installations made from thread, bamboo, cotton, paper and earth, each telling a different story of India. Photograph: (Instagram/@pibindia) Behind the winning exhibition, titled Geographies of Distance: Remembering Home , are five Indian artists who took inspiration from everyday materials, childhood memories and generations-old traditions to explore something we can all relate to: what it means to call a place home. Here are the five artists and the fascinating stories behind their creations. 1. Sumakshi Singh: A house recreated in thread Artwork: Permanent Address Imagine walking into a house that is no longer there. That is the experience Sumakshi Singh creates with Permanent Address , an intricate, life-size reconstruction of her family home in Delhi. The artist has recreated the house using embroidered thread and water-soluble fabric. Artist Sumakshi Singh recreated her childhood home in Delhi using delicate white threads, preserving memories of a house that no longer exists. Photograph: (Instagram/@ abirpothi ) The house was built in 1951 by Singh’s grandparents, who came to India during Partition. It became the venue for family weddings, reunions and childhood sleepovers. It was also where she spent afternoons learning to knit and embroider with her grandmother. Years later, when the house was demolished, the same craft helped her recreate the place she had always called home. 2. Asim Waqif: Bamboo that tells a story of changing cities Artwork: Chaal Using 12 tonnes of bamboo sourced largely from Assam and West Bengal, artist and architect Asim Waqif built a 30-foot-high structure in Venice without using a single nut or bolt. The bamboo pieces are bent and tied together, forming a structure that resembles the scaffolding that supports buildings across Indian cities. Made using 12 tonnes of bamboo sourced largely from Assam and West Bengal, Asim Waqif’s installation highlights traditional building materials and craftsmanship. Photograph: (Instagram/ @indiainvenice ) The choice of material is central to the artwork. Bamboo has long been used in traditional construction, but modern building practices increasingly favour materials such as steel and aluminium. Waqif’s installation draws attention to this shift and the risk of losing traditional skills, such as bending and tying bamboo to build scaffolding. 3. Ranjani Shettar: A garden suspended in the air Artwork: Under the Same Sky In contrast to Waqif’s towering structure, Ranjani Shettar’s installation feels like stepping into a floating garden. Inspired by flowers and natural growth, Under the Same Sky features sculptural forms suspended from the ceiling. Shettar created the flower-like sculptures using handwoven cotton fabric, steel and lacquer. Ranjani Shettar’s Under the Same Sky transforms handwoven cotton fabric, steel and lacquer into flower-like sculptures suspended in the air. Photograph: (Instagram/ @pibindia ) Working from her studio near Sagara in Karnataka, Shettar has used these materials for nearly two decades. Her installation allows visitors to experience the garden from within. 4. Skarma Sonam Tashi: Bringing Ladakh’s homes to Venice Artwork: Echoes of Home What does a traditional Ladakhi settlement look like when recreated thousands of kilometres away? Artist Skarma Sonam Tashi offers an answer through Echoes of Home , an installation inspired by the architecture and landscape of Ladakh. Using papier-mâché, cardboard, egg trays and old paper, he creates a miniature settlement that evokes the region’s traditional homes, built using earth, stone and timber. Inspired by Ladakh’s traditional architecture, Skarma Sonam Tashi’s Echoes of Home recreates a miniature settlement using discarded egg trays, cardboard, papier-mâché and old paper. Photograph: (Instagram/ @pibindia ) Growing up in Ladakh, Tashi was familiar with traditional homes built using locally available earth, stone and timber. Designed for the region’s harsh climate, these houses help keep families warm during winter and cool during summer. As concrete and steel buildings increasingly replace traditional homes, his artwork draws attention to generations of knowledge that Ladakh risks losing. 5. Alwar Balasubramaniam: When nature becomes the artist Artworks: Drift and Not Just for Us Sometimes, the most compelling artwork is made from something as familiar as the ground beneath our feet. For these works, artist Alwar Balasubramaniam, also known as Bala, uses clay and soil sourced from rural Tamil Nadu to create sculptural panels. The surfaces are marked by natural cracks and fissures, capturing the effects of time and environmental forces. Rather than smoothing over these imperfections, the artist makes them the focus of the work. Alwar Balasubramaniam’s Drift and Not Just for Us use Tamil Nadu soil to capture nature’s marks and patterns. Photograph: ( Indian Pavillion ) While the artwork was being created, peacocks, monkeys and snakes passed through the work in progress, leaving their marks on it. It is a reminder of the idea behind his work: the earth is home to every living creature. Five artists, one idea of home India returned to the Venice Biennale after seven years with an exhibition built around materials familiar to millions of Indians: bamboo, thread, cotton, paper and earth. Through their creations, the five artists brought stories of Partition, traditional architecture, family memories, craftsmanship and India’s changing landscapes to an international audience. The exhibition celebrated India’s diverse artistic traditions, bringing stories of memory, nature and heritage to a global audience. Photograph: (Instagram/ @pibindia ) With around 4.5 lakh visitors and an award decided by the public, their exhibition showed how stories rooted in everyday Indian life could resonate with people across the world. Sources: India in Venice 'An Indian postcard from Venice: Why a pavilion at ‘Olympics of the art world’ matters' by Trisha Mukherjee & Divya A for The Indian Express, Published on 23 September 2026. items.title: Before Directing Ramayana, Nitesh Tiwari Was an IIT Bombay Grad Who Quit His Tech Job to Write
items.blurb: When Nitesh Tiwari left a software company after four months, he had no film career waiting for him, only an IIT Bombay engineering degree and an interest in writing. Nearly three decades later, he has directed Ramayana: Part 1. Released on 5 November 2026, it travelled to more than 130 countries and crossed ₹1,000 crore in worldwide gross collections in its opening week, according to a Prime Focus investor presentation. Yet Tiwari’s route to the director’s chair began in a college hostel. The campus where storytelling began Tiwari graduated from IIT Bombay in 1996 with a BTech in Metallurgical Engineering. He did not arrive on campus thinking of a career in cinema; its extracurricular culture introduced him to performance and writing. Hostel competitions brought students into theatre, one-act plays and miming. Encouraged by a senior, Tiwari entered the Freshy Miming Competition and won. He then won the senior competition for four consecutive years and directed hostel plays in his third and fourth years. View this post on Instagram A post shared by The Better India (@thebetterindia) He told Hindustan Times in 2022 that the response to his performances sparked his interest in dramatics and writing. Engineering, he said, later helped him think analytically while structuring screenplays. During his third year, he interned at advertising agency RK Swamy BBDO, where he decided to give writing a chance. His experience reflects the influence of campus theatre in shaping creative careers. From software to advertising, then cinema After graduating, Tiwari joined a software company. He kept questioning whether he wanted to do that work for the rest of his life. Four months later, he quit, choosing to try writing before the comfort of a salary made it harder to change direction. He joined FCB Ulka at one-fourth of his software salary, Hindustan Times reported. Three of the five agencies he applied to rejected him. Ulka hired him after a copy test and a poem, despite initially questioning why an IIT graduate wanted to write. Advertising became a substantial career. IIT Bombay’s alumni profile says Tiwari spent 18 years in the industry: four at FCB Ulka, three at Lowe Lintas and 11 at Leo Burnett. He rose to become Chief Creative Officer at Leo Burnett in Mumbai. Advertising taught him to write for audiences and collaborate. After four months at a software company, Tiwari quit to pursue writing before financial security made switching careers harder. Photograph: ( India Today ) His entry into filmmaking was not part of a mapped career plan. Tiwari and fellow advertising professional Vikas Bahl had written Chillar Party but could not find a director willing to take on a film featuring children and a dog. They decided to direct it themselves rather than abandon the script. In a 2019 interview with Scroll, Tiwari described the move as an unplanned step into filmmaking. Released in 2011, Chillar Party won the National Film Award for Best Children's Film and Best Original Screenplay. Tiwari went on to direct Bhoothnath Returns, Dangal and Chhichhore. He also co-wrote Nil Battey Sannata and Bareilly Ki Barfi. His journey is among the engineering graduates who found their way into filmmaking . A much larger canvas Dangal became a defining point in his career. The 2016 film, based on wrestler Mahavir Singh Phogat and his daughters Geeta and Babita, became a major international commercial success, including in China, where it reached audiences well beyond the usual Hindi-film market. Nitesh Tiwari’s filmography spans heartfelt coming-of-age stories, sporting triumphs, family entertainers and ambitious mythological storytelling. Photograph: ( Instagram/@vp_films_0 ) Tiwari received the Filmfare Award for Best Director in 2017, according to IIT Bombay’s alumni profile. Chhichhore, released in 2019, returned him to the campus setting that had shaped his early creative life. His career also reflects the relationship between theatre and cinema in the making of performers and storytellers. His latest assignment, Ramayana, takes that storytelling journey to a different scale, drawing on an epic familiar to audiences across generations. The two-part adaptation brings together a large cast and a global production and distribution effort. The first instalment was released in Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam. Prime Focus’s November 2026 investor presentation described it as the widest global release for an Indian film, with screenings in more than 130 countries and major premium formats including IMAX, Dolby Cinema, ScreenX and 4DX. The company also reported that the film crossed ₹1,000 crore in worldwide gross collections in its opening week. The figures come from the production company’s disclosure. A second instalment is planned. His journey was not an overnight leap from engineering to cinema. It passed through years of advertising, writing and collaboration. It began with a decision to leave a job after four months and give writing a chance; it has since taken him from hostel performances to a film released across continents.
