items.title: This Arunachal Frog Eats Entire Snails & Scientists Just Found It After 5 Years Of Searching
items.blurb: Imagine walking through a forest in the Eastern Himalayas after sunset. The ground is damp, fallen leaves gather beneath towering trees, and the sounds of insects fill the night air. Somewhere among the undergrowth, a tiny frog sits almost unnoticed, blending into its surroundings. In forests like these, some of nature's most fascinating discoveries are easy to miss. And a recent scientific study has brought five such hidden inhabitants into the spotlight. Researchers from the University of Delhi and Harvard University have identified five previously unknown species of horned frogs in Arunachal Pradesh, following five years of fieldwork in the Eastern Himalayas. The discovery has also revealed something unusual about one of them: it feeds on land snails, making it the first known snail-eating frog recorded in India. The research offers a fascinating glimpse into the biodiversity that India's forests continue to hold. Meet the five newly discovered frogs All five species belong to the genus Jingophrys , commonly known as diminutive horned frogs. These tiny to medium-sized amphibians are distinguished by horn-like projections of skin around their eyes, which give them their distinctive appearance. The Tanii horned frog (Jingophrys taniitatii) is named after the Tanii tribe of Arunachal Pradesh, incorporating the Apatani word for frogs and toads. Photograph: ( The Times of India ) The five newly identified species are: Tanii horned frog ( Jingophrys taniitatii ): Named after the Tanii tribe of Arunachal Pradesh, the name also incorporates 'tatii', the Apatani word for frogs and toads. Snail-eating horned frog ( Jingophrys tanogogo ): Named after the Apatani word for snails, this species has an especially unusual diet. Siang horned frog ( Jingophrys siangensis ): Named after the Siang region of Arunachal Pradesh, where it was discovered. Hrdy's horned frog ( Jingophrys hrdy ): Named in recognition of a long-time supporter of herpetological research and conservation biology at Harvard University. Wu-Larson's horned frog ( Jingophrys wularsoni ): Also named to recognise supporters of research and conservation at Harvard. The names of three species acknowledge the region's local communities, language and geography, while the other two honour individuals who have supported scientific research. A frog that eats snails, shells and all! Among the five discoveries, Jingophrys tanogogo stands out for its unusual feeding behaviour. While examining the species, researchers used advanced three-dimensional micro-CT imaging to study its internal anatomy. They found entire land snail shells inside the frog's gut. The snail-eating horned frog (Jingophrys tanogogo) is India's first recorded frog species known to consume land snails, shells and all. Photograph: ( Deccan Herald ) This makes it the first known snail-eating frog recorded in India and the first documented instance of snail-eating behaviour in the family Megophryidae. It is a remarkable finding because it expands what scientists know about the feeding habits of this group of amphibians. Five years of research in challenging terrain Identifying these frogs was no easy task. The research team included Sonali Garg, S D Biju, Tage Tajo, Radhakrishna Upadhyaya K, and James Hanken, who carried out extensive explorations across the Eastern Himalayas. The researchers encountered temperatures as low as minus 4 degrees Celsius while navigating the mountainous terrain. Since these frogs are nocturnal, much of the fieldwork involved searching for them at night, often without a place to stay. Researchers used advanced 3D micro-CT imaging to examine the frogs' anatomy, discovering entire land snail shells inside one species' gut. Photograph: ( The Hindu ) Local tribal communities also played an important role, sharing their knowledge of the region and supporting the researchers during their field explorations. Beyond identifying new species, the team used DNA analysis to understand their evolutionary history. Their findings suggest that the diversification of these frogs coincided with the rise of the Himalayan mountain ranges and the intensification of the Asian monsoon millions of years ago. Why these discoveries matter The findings draw attention to the Eastern Himalayas as an important centre of biodiversity and evolution. The number of Jingophrys species recorded in India has increased seven-fold through this research, while the known diversity of the genus worldwide has more than doubled. Yet, there is still much to learn. Some of these frogs are extremely secretive and appear in remote forests only during short breeding seasons. Further research will be needed to understand their ecology, behaviour and conservation needs. The five-year research involved night-time explorations across the challenging terrain of the Eastern Himalayas, with local tribal communities helping researchers navigate the region. Photograph: ( Indian Expresss ) For now, these five discoveries offer a reminder of how much life remains undocumented in India's forests. Sometimes, finding an entirely new species does not require looking beyond a distant wilderness. It simply requires looking a little closer at the world beneath our feet. Sources: 'New frog species found in Arunachal, Keralam scientist part of team' by K S Sreejith for The New Indian Express, Published on 14 November 2026. items.title: Once Rare in Ujani, 10 Lakh Deccan Mahseer Get a Fresh Chance Through a 10-Year Plan
items.blurb: A fish that had nearly disappeared from Maharashtra’s Ujani Reservoir decades ago is getting another chance to swim in its waters. The Deccan Mahseer, once found in abundance in the Bhima River basin, had become increasingly rare by the 1990s as pollution, invasive fish species and destructive fishing practices took a toll on the reservoir’s native aquatic life. Now, in October 2026, the Bombay Natural History Society (BNHS), with support from the Cipla Foundation and Tata Power, released 45 lakh (4.5 million) native fish fingerlings, including 10 lakh Deccan Mahseer (Tor khudree), popularly known as the ‘Tiger of the River’, alongside more than 21,000 aquatic plants into Maharashtra’s Ujani wetland near Bhigwan. According to BNHS, the restoration programme responds to decades of ecological degradation in Ujani, where invasive fish, deteriorating water quality and destructive fishing practices have contributed to the decline of native species. Why did the fish disappear? Ujani Reservoir, formed by the Ujani Dam on the Bhima River, is an important freshwater ecosystem spanning parts of Pune, Solapur and Ahilyanagar districts. Over the years, however, its aquatic biodiversity has come under pressure from invasive fish, pollution and fishing methods that capture even young fish before they can reproduce. According to the BNHS, around 35 native fish species have become locally extinct in the reservoir, while another 40 are at risk of disappearing. According to the BNHS, around 35 native fish species have become locally extinct in the reservoir, while another 40 are at risk of disappearing. Photograph: (Rajeev Raghavan) Invasive species such as suckermouth catfish, tilapia and African catfish have spread through its waters. The BNHS-led restoration programme has also identified the impact of invasive aquatic vegetation , which can obstruct waterways, affect oxygen levels and compete with native plants. The scale of the intervention reflects the extent of the problem. BNHS and local fisheries societies have removed more than 178 tonnes of invasive fish from the reservoir over the past year. Additionally, nearly 6,500 tonnes of invasive vegetation, including water hyacinth, Ipomoea and Prosopis, have been cleared from approximately 2,000 hectares of the catchment area. The October stocking programme included 10 lakh Indian major carps, comprising rohu, catla and mrigal, alongside more than 22 lakh fingerlings of other native species, including kavdas, nukta and bobari. What makes the Deccan Mahseer important? The Deccan Mahseer, also known as the blue-fin mahseer, is a freshwater fish belonging to the carp family. Its historic distribution includes the Krishna River system and its tributaries across parts of Maharashtra, Karnataka, and Telangana. A 2019 scientific review, titled Mahseer (Tor spp.) Fishes of the World: Status, Challenges and Opportunities for Conservation , published in the journal Reviews in Fish Biology and Fisheries, examined the distribution, conservation status and threats facing mahseer species. This is the Deccan Mahseer, revered as Lord Vithoba's beloved "Devmaasa". Found in Indrayani river, it is now endangered due to pollution & deadly water hyacinth growth on Anand Doha. A case of authorities' indifference😢 ##goodbadugly #saverivers Image: iNaturalist (1/2) https://t.co/5aTWC0UhK4 — Pune River Revival (@PuneRivers) May 22, 2024 The researchers identified the northern and central Western Ghats, particularly the Krishna River system, as the historical range of the Deccan Mahseer. Its tributaries include the Indrayani, Mula-Mutha, Koyna, Tungabhadra and Panchaganga. The review also highlighted how artificial propagation and large-scale fish stocking since the 1970s expanded the species' distribution beyond its original range. Some introduced populations have even shown invasive characteristics, affecting native fish populations in other river systems. Another study, published in Fisheries Research in 2011, examined the sustainability of Deccan Mahseer fisheries in the Western Ghats using catch data collected with the participation of local fishers. Researchers Rajeev Raghavan, Anvar Ali, Neelesh Dahanukar and Alison Rosser studied six fishing sites and found that catches frequently included immature fish. Their assessment also indicated that exploitation rates exceeded sustainable levels at most of the sites studied. A 10-year plan to bring the fish back The Ujani restoration programme included a dedicated partnership between BNHS and Tata Power for the conservation of the Deccan Mahseer. Under the arrangement, Tata Power has committed to supplying 10 lakh mahseer fingerlings over 10 years. The fish are being bred with support from its facility at Valvan in Lonavala. View this post on Instagram A post shared by BNHS 💚 Wildlife Conservation (@bombaynaturalhistorysociety) According to BNHS's October 2026 conservation newsletter, Dr Unmesh Katwate, head of the BNHS Wetland Eco-Restoration Project, visited the facility on 9 October to assess the available fingerling stock and preparations for their release. The newsletter also records a separate initial release of 8,000 fingerlings near Palasnath Temple in Ujani Reservoir on 22 October. The site was selected after considering its depth, water quality and habitat conditions. The organisation is also working with local fisheries societies and government departments to encourage more sustainable fishing practices. For Ujani, the return of the Deccan Mahseer is therefore part of a larger restoration exercise. Whether the mahseer can establish a self-sustaining population in the reservoir will become clearer through continued monitoring in the coming years. items.title: From Washing Dishes to Singing for Millions: Talwiinder Gets Candid About How He Taught Himself Music
items.blurb: What do you do when you want to become a musician, but your rehearsal room is a fast-food outlet and your practice time begins after the last customer has left? For more than four years, Talwiinder's answer was to sing while washing dishes and closing Subway. He started working there in Class 10, fitting riyaaz (music practice) around customer orders and closing duties. Without formal music training, he used the time after serving customers to practise his singing. Today, his music has travelled far beyond that counter. ‘Pal Pal’, made with Afusic and Ali Soomro, caught the attention of British DJ and producer Fred again.., who played the track during a livestream. Talwiinder saw it just like everyone else watching. It was, he says, “a beautiful moment for the South Asian music scene”. Between those closing shifts and the livestream were years of teaching himself music, writing songs and continuing to create despite rejection from music labels. From serving customers to writing songs Talwiinder has been singing since he was three or four, but he says the decision to build a life around music came when he began writing songs of his own. Singing was something he loved; songwriting gave that love somewhere to go . The ‘Pal Pal’ livestream moment connected a Punjabi collaboration with audiences beyond its listening community. Photograph: ( Instagram/@talwiinder ) “The moment I started to write my own songs, I knew I had to release these tracks for people who need it more than me,” he tells The Better India . “Once I got into songwriting, I knew this is what I want to do for the rest of my life.” There was no ready-made route into the industry. He spent more than four years at Subway, starting in Class 10, and remembers the job fondly for what it taught him about people. “It taught me communication, reading people's energy and having one-on-one conversations with customers to the point where I knew their whole order the moment they stepped in the store,” he says. He learnt to run the store by himself. When the rush was over, he had time alone with his thoughts. “That alone time was often used to do riyaaz while cleaning dishes and closing the store,” he says. “I loved every bit of that job and never felt like I wanted to quit.” His music moves between Punjabi and international listening spaces, opening possibilities for cross-cultural collaboration. Interestingly, someone who once spent hours interacting with customers now prefers to keep conversations brief. He says he prefers texting to phone calls and often avoids conversations because talking for too long tires his throat and voice. He likes to “talk with eyes” and use very few words. He even has a WhatsApp display picture that reads, “Don't call me, text me.” Through the songs he writes, however, Talwiinder communicates with millions of listeners. Learning how to express himself through music has involved years of listening to and understanding his own voice. How he taught himself music Without formal music training, Talwiinder learnt by making songs and returning to them. He advises beginners with a laptop or computer to invest in a home-recording setup, which he estimates can cost around $150 to $200, rather than waiting for a professional studio or teacher. “Record yourself as much as you can,” he says. “You will understand your voice better. When the time comes and you're in a proper studio with top-notch equipment, you won't be so lost, but excited to go full beast mode.” For listeners discovering Punjabi music abroad, Talwiinder offers an entry point into Punjabi sounds. Listening to these recordings helps a singer recognise what needs work and gradually develop a sound of their own. It is something aspiring musicians can begin doing with basic equipment at home. Over time, Talwiinder has also learnt when to stop working on a song and let listeners hear it. He does not believe there is a magical point at which a track becomes perfect. “The song is never ready; there will always be something that can be added or taken out,” he says. “You have to trust your gut and give your 100% in stitching the song together, and once it's out, make peace with it and move on to the next song.” With every release comes a public tally of streams, views and likes, but Talwiinder says he has never made numbers the measure of his work. He recalls gaining more than four million Instagram followers in a month without paid promotions. He says he has never bought fake views or likes, or followed trends. His focus, he says, is on doing justice to the music, while listeners decide whether to return to it. When he does not feel like starting something new, he returns to his unfinished tracks. “I have way too many unfinished songs,” he says. He chooses his favourites and starts finishing them, turning a creative block into a chance to reopen old work. When music labels turned him down The years were not without rejection. Talwiinder remembers approaching labels that did not want to associate with his music. Among the tracks he mentions is ‘Khayaal’. The singer's visual aesthetic draws from alternative music culture rather than conventional Punjabi entertainment imagery. “They told me indirectly and did not want to associate with my music,” he says. “Funny thing is I still see those labels coming back and asking to work together.” He kept making music, including songs that did not immediately find their moment. ‘Haseen’ was written and recorded in 2019 but released six years later. He says he would not change his older music simply because he has grown as an artist. “I believe good music does not have an expiration date,” he says. A song does not lose its value, in his view, because it has been waiting in a folder. With ‘Pal Pal’, Talwiinder experienced what it was like for his music to reach someone he had not expected. The collaboration with Afusic and Ali Soomro caught the attention of Fred again.. When the British DJ played the track during a livestream, Talwiinder did not hear about it through a label or a carefully arranged announcement. He saw it on the stream, like everybody else. “It caught me by surprise,” he says. “It was a beautiful moment for the South Asian music scene.” With his signature face paint and unconventional styling, Talwiinder has carved out a recognisable space in contemporary music. Having experienced rejection himself, Talwiinder now wants to help other aspiring musicians find people they can work with. Asked what he would do if a young artist arrived with little money and no industry connections, Talwiinder says he would first listen. If the work felt genuine and original, he would connect the artist with his community and suggest collaborators, giving them somewhere to belong. For someone who spent years practising after work and learning to make music on his own, being able to offer another young artist a place to begin is something he now looks forward to.

Britain needs to regain control of its immigration system after the chaos of Brexit. Yet sixteen years after David Cameron’s ‘tens of thousands’ pledge, six prime ministers and ten home secretaries have overseen wild swings in immigration numbers with net migration now set to fall below zero.

Britain faces serious demographic and economic challenges, and urgently needs a proper immigration plan to support our economy and public services.

The fall in net migration is mainly a result of changes made by the previous Conservative government. We now need to go even further with a legally binding annual cap, set by parliament, at a far lower level.

British and European people are leaving in their droves because of Labour’s high taxes whilst non-EU immigration remains far too high. Mass low-skilled immigration must end completely as it is bad for our economy and corrosive to our society.

But, said the enthusiastic member of the creator ranks, he would continue because he was trying to reach people “where they were at”.

items.title: What’s with Jan van Eyck’s tiny hands? | Brief letters
items.blurb:
A riddle or bad draughtsmanship? | Trump’s Nvidia deal | Not a flavour to savour | Melania’s $150 photos | Word Wheel winner

In her feature on Jan van Eyck’s portraits (Tricks! Traps! Riddles! Jan van Eyck’s portraits look vividly real – but are full of secret messages. What do they mean?, 19 November), Charlotte Higgins noted that “the precision of his physiognomies is dizzying”, but did not pick up on the Flemish master’s disproportionately small rendering of his sitters’ hands. (Nor did Jonathan Jones mention this in his review of the Van Eyck exhibition at the National Gallery.) Was this another of his “riddles” or just poor draughtsmanship?
Bryan Biggs
Liverpool

• Trump told CNBC that he “made the deal” with the Nvidia board (Huang returns to Nvidia hotseat as board bows to Trump pressure, 24 November). A deal, as the self-styled deal-maker extraordinaire will know, involves each party getting and giving something. We can see what the US president got, but what did he give?
Mark de Brunner
Burn Bridge, North Yorkshire

items.title: Influencers Behaving Badly at No 10? Burnham could have worse problems | Emma Brockes
items.blurb:
For all the fuss, it makes perfect sense for the PM to engage young people through TikTokers. He’ll have the last laugh on this one

These are dangerous times to be a prime minister. So it is perhaps reassuring that the trouble into which Andy Burnham barrelled this week is so old school as to be almost soothing. Four months into his premiership, Burnham has arrived early at that rite of passage: the catastrophic attempt to engage with popular culture and subsequent category-5 storm in a teacup. After footage emerged of Influencers Behaving Badly at Downing Street, Burnham, in my view, has come out of the whole thing in surprisingly good shape.

To recap: earlier this month, Burnham held a reception for social media influencers, one of whom, Luke Hamnett, was permitted to film himself doing the Hugh Grant dance from Love Actually before sitting down to interview the prime minister. Meanwhile, self-described “presenter, podcaster, idiot” Max Balegde filmed himself outside the door of No 10 miming what, in the words of the Daily Mail as it geared up to go the full Judge Pickles, “appeared to be a viral meme song”. These words were “bomboclaat pussywagon chicken nuggets”, which, as the Telegraph took a breath from its own meltdown to explain, turns on “a Jamaican profanity popularised online”.

Emma Brockes is a Guardian columnist
